Suppose a rectangle $r$ is contained in the chosen fundamental square. Write its southwest and northeast corners as $x_1,x_2\in\mathbf x$ and its northwest and southeast corners as $y_1,y_2\in\mathbf y$; all other state points are common. In $J(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)-J(\mathbf y,\mathbf y)$ the common-point terms cancel, the ordered corner pair contributes $1$, and each point of $\mathbf x$ strictly inside $r$ contributes twice, once against each changed corner. Thus this difference is $1+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. In $2J(\mathbf x,\mathbb O)-2J(\mathbf y,\mathbb O)$ the same cancellation leaves twice the number of $O$-markings in $r$. Substituting these two counts into [F1] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Replacing every $O$ by $X$ gives the stated formula for $M_{\mathbb X}$. [F1, construct, algebra]

For a marking set $P\in\{\mathbb O,\mathbb X\}$, write $M_P(\mathbf x)=J(\mathbf x-P,\mathbf x-P)+1$ and let $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)$ denote the northwest grid vertex of the cell containing the $i$th mark, read on the bottom edge when that cell is in the top row. Let $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P}$ be the state consisting of these vertices. Expanding the $J$ formula in [F1] gives $M_P(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P})=\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}-\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_j\}-\#\{(i,j):P_i<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}+\#\{(i,j):P_i<P_j\}+1.$ For distinct $i,j$ with neither mark in the top row, all four inequalities are equivalent and their signed contributions cancel. If $P_j$ is in the top row, the second and fourth inequalities are equivalent and the first and third are false; if $P_i$ is in the top row, the first and second inequalities are equivalent and the third and fourth are false. These contributions also cancel. For $i=j$, the only inequality that can hold is $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_i$, and it holds exactly for the unique mark in the top row. The displayed count is therefore $-1+1=0$, proving $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X})=0$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

For two complementary rectangles $r$ and $r'$ with the same vertical edges, let $v$ be their common width, counted in column strips. The one-$O$- and one-$X$-per-column conditions in [F2] give $n_{\mathbb O}(r)+n_{\mathbb O}(r')=v$ and $n_{\mathbb X}(r)+n_{\mathbb X}(r')=v$. The state has one point on each of the $v-1$ vertical circles strictly between those two edges, so $\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)+\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r')=v-1$. If the formula of step 1.2 holds for $r$ from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$, these three equalities give the formula for $r'$ from $\mathbf y$ to $\mathbf x$ by subtraction. The same argument applies to complementary rectangles sharing horizontal edges, counting rows instead of columns. Of the four torus rectangles for the two states, one lies in the fundamental square; successive horizontal or vertical complementations reach each of the other three, so the formulas hold for every torus rectangle. [F2, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Subtract the $M_{\mathbb X}$ change from the $M_{\mathbb O}$ change and divide by two. The constant terms and state-interior terms cancel, giving $\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)}2-\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)}2=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The common normalization $-(n-1)/2$ in $A_G$ cancels, proving the rectangle-change formula and that all differences of $A_G$ are integers. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

The row and column connections from $O$ to $X$ and back form one $n$-cycle by [F2]. Equivalently, the relative permutation between $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ and $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O}$ is an $n$-cycle. Hence this value is integral. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 1.3, choose, algebra]

Any two grid states correspond to permutations, and a finite product of transpositions carries one to the other. Each transposition gives a rectangle transition. Step 3.1 shows that $A_G$ changes by an integer at every transition; since one state has integral Alexander value by step 3.2, all grid states do. [step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎

Work in the smooth category inherited from the oriented-link convention. In particular, an embedded bridge witness disk means the image of a smooth rank-two embedding of a planar disk, with ordinary smooth boundary or smooth transverse corners at its two marked endpoints; smoothness at a boundary or corner means local smooth extension in its charts. Witness parametrizations can be chosen for the finite disk families. This category convention does not require the knot arcs to meet the Heegaard surface transversely: tangential smooth crossings remain permitted.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $h$, let $k\ge1$, and put $m=h+k-1$. A **handlebody** is a compact three-manifold that is a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph. A **$2k$-pointed Heegaard diagram for $S^3$** consists of a splitting $S^3=U_{\alpha}\cup_{\Sigma}U_{\beta}$ into handlebodies, two systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves on $\Sigma$ that bound pairwise disjoint properly embedded disks in $U_{\alpha}$ and $U_{\beta}$, respectively, cutting each handlebody into exactly $k$ three-balls, and two ordered sets of distinct points $\mathbf w=(w_1,\ldots,w_k)$ and $\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_k)$ disjoint from the curves. Curves from different systems intersect transversely in finitely many points. Each component of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$ contains exactly one $w$-point and exactly one $z$-point. The diagram also includes trivial arc systems in the two handlebodies: the $\alpha$-arcs join $w_i$ to $z_i$, and the $\beta$-arcs join $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$, with indices modulo $k$. Each system is disjoint from its compression disks and is simultaneously boundary parallel: its arcs cobound pairwise disjoint embedded disks with arcs in the corresponding components of the attaching-system complement on $\Sigma$. Thus each ball obtained by compression contains one unknotted arc. Together the arcs form an oriented knot, oriented from $w_i$ to $z_i$ in $U_{\alpha}$ and from $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$ in $U_{\beta}$. The diagram is **compatible with $K$** when this knot is orientation-preservingly ambient isotopic to $K$. For a grid diagram, compatibility uses the row and column orientation fixed in the grid definition, with $w$-points at $O$ and $z$-points at $X$. For a grid representing one knot, the basepoint pairs can be numbered cyclically in reverse order of travel along the oriented knot so that $w_i,z_i$ lie in the same component $A_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and $w_i,z_{i+1}$ lie in the same component $B_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$.

Comparisons of these embedded diagrams allow **orientation-preserving diagram isomorphisms**: an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ carrying the two handlebodies, their oriented Heegaard surface, the two attaching systems, the ordered $w,z$ points, and the two simultaneously boundary-parallel arc systems to the corresponding data. Equivalently one may specify the surface isomorphism together with its compatible collared extensions over both handlebodies carrying those arcs. The attaching systems are carried as systems; reordering their curve factors induces the corresponding product identification. Comparisons also allow **arc normalizations in the fixed splitting**: a smooth isotopy of the represented oriented knot, supported near the ordered marks and fixing each mark, during which every open connecting arc stays in its original handlebody and the two simultaneous boundary-parallel witness systems are retained or replaced by embedded witnesses for those same arcs. The surface, attaching curves, marked points and compression disks stay fixed. Such a normalization may replace a tangential marked crossing by a transverse one; the original data are not required to have neat arcs. This is a change of knot representative relative to the fixed surface, not a diagram isomorphism carrying both objects. Analytic and assigned grading data depending on the fixed surface diagram can be kept identical; the corresponding generator and disk-count identification is then the identity. Existence of normalizations with the required witnesses is a separate geometric assertion, not part of this definition. Such a comparison transports the represented oriented knot and any specified Seifert surface as well. For analytic data, it transports $j$, the surface area form, all chosen divisor neighborhoods and $J_t$ by the induced symmetric-product diffeomorphism. The comparison maps on generators and disk classes are their pushforwards under this map; compatibility with the count differential is a mathematical property to be proved. No identity action is part of this convention, even when the ambient diffeomorphism is isotopic to the identity.

The $m$-fold symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)=\Sigma^m/S_m$ is the space of unordered $m$-tuples of points of $\Sigma$, where $S_m$ permutes coordinates. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ be the quotient map. The product tori are the images $\mathbb T_{\alpha}=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_m)$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_m)$. Their intersection points are the generators. A **Whitney disk class** $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps from a disk to $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ whose two boundary arcs lie on $\mathbb T_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}$ and whose endpoints are $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions with coefficients equal to local multiplicities. Write $n_{w_i}(\phi)$ and $n_{z_i}(\phi)$ for its local multiplicities at the marked points. An almost complex structure $J$ on $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ is a smooth endomorphism of the tangent bundle with $J^2=-1$. Fix a complex structure $j$ and an area form on $\Sigma$. For $m>0$, choose a smooth path $\mathbb J=(J_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ of nearly symmetric almost complex structures, constant near $t=0,1$: each $J_t$ agrees with the induced integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(j)$ on a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and of every divisor $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ for a chosen interior point $p$ of every complementary region, including every marked point, and tames the form descended from the product area form off that neighborhood. The path is a sufficiently small perturbation in this class. For $m=0$ the symmetric product is a point. Local multiplicities are intersection numbers with these divisors; positivity is a mathematical property to be proved, not an additional choice of disk counts. A $\mathbb J$-holomorphic strip representative is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ satisfying $\partial_{\tau}u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with $u(\tau,0)\in\mathbb T_{\alpha}$, $u(\tau,1)\in\mathbb T_{\beta}$, and limits $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ as $\tau\to-\infty,+\infty$. Translation in $\tau$ defines an $\mathbb R$-action. The Maslov index $\mu(\phi)$ is the Fredholm index of the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at a representative of $\phi$; the relative Maslov grading convention is $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=\mu(\phi)-2\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_{w_i}(\phi)$, up to one overall additive constant.

A **periodic domain** is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of full $\alpha$- and $\beta$-curves; its local multiplicity at a marked point is the coefficient of the containing region. The pointed diagram is **admissible** when every nonzero periodic domain with $n_{w_i}=0$ for all $i$ has at least one positive and at least one negative region coefficient. A path $\mathbb J$ is **regular for a set of disk classes** when the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at every holomorphic-strip representative in those classes is surjective. For a path regular on the classes used, let $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)$ be the space of strip representatives. If, for each generator $\mathbf x$, only finitely many pairs $(\mathbf y,\phi)$ with $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing$, $\mu(\phi)=1$, and $n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0$ for every $i$ occur, and each quotient is finite, the multipointed full filtered minus module is the free module over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_k]$ generated by $\mathbb T_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb T_{\beta}$, with differential
$$\partial^-\mathbf x=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y),\;\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing\\\mu(\phi)=1,\; n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0\ \forall i}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)\,U_1^{n_{w_1}(\phi)}\cdots U_k^{n_{w_k}(\phi)}\mathbf y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is the count modulo two of the zero-dimensional quotient when it is finite. Quotienting by all $U_i$ leaves the fully blocked multipointed chain complex (the hat chain complex when $k=1$), with terms only from classes satisfying $n_{w_i}=0$ for every $i$; its Alexander-filtered associated-graded complex further retains only classes with every $n_{z_i}=0$. The relative Alexander grading convention is $A(\mathbf x)-A(\mathbf y)=\sum_i n_{z_i}(\phi)-\sum_i n_{w_i}(\phi)$, with an overall additive constant. Each $U_i$ lowers Maslov grading by two and Alexander filtration by one. In a grid diagram, $\Sigma=T^2$, $h=1$, $k=n$, and $m=n$; the horizontal circles are the $\alpha$-curves, the vertical circles are the $\beta$-curves, and the $w$-points and $z$-points are the $O$- and $X$-markings respectively.

derivations.claim: Regard the grid torus as the standard Heegaard torus separating the two solid tori of $S^3$, with horizontal circles meridians of the first and vertical circles meridians of the second. The $n$ parallel meridian disks in either solid torus cut it into $n$ balls, one for each row or column annulus. Push the row $O$-to-$X$ arcs into the first solid torus and the column $X$-to-$O$ arcs into the second. Their pushing disks lie in disjoint row or column annuli and are disjoint from the compression disks, so each arc system is simultaneously boundary parallel as required by [F2]. The over/under convention is vertical over horizontal, exactly [F1]'s link. Thus these data represent the same oriented knot and satisfy the topological part of the multipointed definition; it remains to prove its admissibility condition. [F1, F2, given, construct]

Let $p_{ij}$ be the coefficient of cell $R_{ij}$ in a periodic domain $P$. Because $\partial P$ is a sum of whole horizontal and vertical circles, the coefficient jump across a vertical circle is independent of the row, and the jump across a horizontal circle is independent of the column. Fix reference indices $i_0,j_0$ and set $a_i=p_{i,j_0}$ and $b_j=p_{i_0,j}-p_{i_0,j_0}$. Summing the constant jumps from the reference row and column gives $p_{ij}=a_i+b_j$ for every cell. Since the marking permutation in [F1] is one cycle, number its basepoint pairs in reverse order of knot travel so that row region $A_i$ contains $w_i,z_i$ and column region $B_i$ contains $w_i,z_{i+1}$, as allowed by the convention in [F2]. Then $P=\sum_i a_iA_i+\sum_i b_iB_i$, with local multiplicities $n_{w_i}(P)=a_i+b_i$ and $n_{z_i}(P)=a_i+b_{i-1}$. [F1, F2, construct]

Suppose $P$ is periodic and all $n_{w_i}(P)=0$. Then $b_i=-a_i$, so $n_{z_i}(P)=a_i-a_{i-1}$ and $\sum_i n_{z_i}(P)=0$. If one $n_{z_i}(P)$ is nonzero, these integer multiplicities include both a positive and a negative value; each is a region coefficient at the corresponding $X$-cell, so $P$ has both signs. [step 1.2, algebra]

If all $n_{z_i}(P)$ also vanish, then all $a_i$ are the same integer $c$ and all $b_i=-c$. Hence $P=c(\sum_iA_i-\sum_iB_i)=0$, because each of the two sums is the whole torus with coefficient one. Thus a nonzero periodic domain with zero $O$-multiplicity cannot have all $X$-multiplicities zero, and step 2.1 proves it has both signs. By [F2], the grid diagram is admissible. [F2, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

The **grid-complex algorithm** takes a finite encoded grid and a mode from $\{\mathrm{tilde},\mathrm{minus\text{-}associated\text{-}graded},\mathrm{minus\text{-}filtered}\}$. It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

For a valid knot grid, number the horizontal and vertical circles $1,\ldots,n$ and enumerate all permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ in lexicographic order. The state for a permutation $\sigma$ consists of the $n$ intersections $(i,\sigma(i))$. For each ordered pair of states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, if they agree in other than exactly $n-2$ points, add no rectangle terms. Otherwise enumerate the at most two torus rectangles with the four nonshared state points as corners, retain those whose interiors contain no point of $\mathbf x$, and apply the selected mode. In the full filtered mode, each term drops filtration by $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$; the associated-graded mode retains precisely the terms with zero drop, which are the rectangles with no $X$-marking:

1. **Tilde mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2$. Count a retained rectangle with coefficient $1$ exactly when its interior contains no $O$- or $X$-marking.
2. **Associated-graded minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count a retained rectangle exactly when its interior contains no $X$-marking, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$.
3. **Full filtered minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count every retained rectangle, regardless of its $X$-markings, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$. Use the grid Alexander value for each state and assign filtration drop $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$ to this term.

Return the ordered state list, the mode and coefficient ring, the exact differential matrix obtained by summing coefficients modulo two, the state Maslov and Alexander values, and the filtration data for the full filtered mode. The algorithm returns this finite presentation only; its identification with knot Floer homology and its independence of the chosen grid are separate theorems. The factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is not multiplied into the output.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid of grid number $n$ representing one oriented knot, and let $M_{\mathbb O}$, $M_{\mathbb X}$, and $A_G$ be the functions defined from its finite point sets and the pair-counting function $J$. Then $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integer-valued, and every rectangle $r$ from a grid state $\mathbf x$ to a grid state $\mathbf y$ satisfies $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb X}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Consequently $A_G$ is integer-valued and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$.

derivations.claim: For two successive rectangles $r_1,r_2$, let $\psi=r_1+r_2$ be their cellwise sum as a two-chain, and let $\mathbf x,\mathbf z$ be the initial and terminal states. The state permutation changes by one transposition at each rectangle. If $\mathbf x\ne\mathbf z$, their relative permutation is either a product of two disjoint transpositions, so four points move, or a $3$-cycle, so three points move. These are the only nonidentity products of two transpositions. [F1, given, algebra]

For a counted rectangle $r$ the interior contains no state point, so [F3] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The coefficient $\prod_iU_i^{O_i(r)}$ lowers Maslov degree by $2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ by [F2]; hence the full term has degree $-1$. [F2, F3, algebra]

In the four-point case, the two transpositions are disjoint and commute. Exchanging their order gives the alternate intermediate state; the first rectangle in one decomposition has the same support as the second rectangle in the other, and conversely. Thus both decompositions have the same two rectangle interiors and are empty together. No third decomposition is possible, because the four distinct changing corners must be paired into the same two disjoint transpositions fixed by the endpoint permutation and the domain boundary. [step 1.1, construct]

In the three-point case, following the boundary of $\psi$ gives a six-corner region with five right-angle corners and one reflex corner of angle $270^\circ$; every cell coefficient is zero or one. At the reflex corner the boundary can be cut in exactly two ways into two rectangles. Each cut gives the required intermediate grid state, and the resulting interiors contain no additional state point because any such point would already lie in the interior of one of the original empty rectangles. The six-corner boundary has no other concave corner at which to make a cut, so these are exactly the two decompositions. [step 1.1, construct]

If $\mathbf x=\mathbf z$, the two rectangles reverse the same state transposition and their union is a periodic annulus. If the annulus were not thin, its transverse width would include at least two grid strips; the interior would then contain a state point on an intervening grid circle, contradicting emptiness. Hence every returning domain is one of the $n$ horizontal thin annuli, each occupying one row strip, or one of the $n$ vertical thin annuli, each occupying one column strip. Conversely, the two state points on the boundary circles of any one-row strip split that strip into two empty rectangles, and the same holds for every one-column strip, so all $2n$ listed annuli occur as returning composites. Each contains exactly one $O$ and one $X$ by the row and column marking conditions, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, the horizontal annulus through the row of $O_i$ contributes $U_i$, and the vertical annulus through its column also contributes $U_i$. Every $O_i$ therefore occurs twice among all returning domains, and the total is zero over $\mathbb F_2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

In either non-annular case the two decompositions have the same cellwise domain $\psi$. A forbidden $O$- or $X$-marking occurs in one rectangle of a decomposition exactly when its cell has positive coefficient in $\psi$; hence a mode excluding that marking accepts either both decompositions or neither. For each $O_i$, the exponent in the product coefficient is its multiplicity in $\psi$, so the two accepted terms have the same monomial. They cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

The Alexander change in [F3] is $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. Multiplication by the coefficient lowers filtration by $n_{\mathbb O}(r)$, so the output filtration is $A_G(\mathbf x)-n_{\mathbb X}(r)$. Thus the full filtered term drops by exactly $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$, and the tilde and associated-graded modes, which count only rectangles with $n_{\mathbb X}(r)=0$, preserve Alexander grading. [F2, F3, algebra] ∎

It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

For a valid knot grid, number the horizontal and vertical circles $1,\ldots,n$ and enumerate all permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ in lexicographic order. The state for a permutation $\sigma$ consists of the $n$ intersections $(i,\sigma(i))$. For each ordered pair of states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, if they agree in other than exactly $n-2$ points, add no rectangle terms. Otherwise enumerate the at most two torus rectangles with the four nonshared state points as corners, retain those whose interiors contain no point of $\mathbf x$, and apply the selected mode. In the full filtered mode, each term drops filtration by $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$; the associated-graded mode retains precisely the terms with zero drop, which are the rectangles with no $X$-marking:

1. **Tilde mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2$. Count a retained rectangle with coefficient $1$ exactly when its interior contains no $O$- or $X$-marking.
2. **Associated-graded minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count a retained rectangle exactly when its interior contains no $X$-marking, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$.
3. **Full filtered minus mode.** Work over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$, with each $U_i$ of Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$. Count every retained rectangle, regardless of its $X$-markings, with coefficient $\prod_{i=1}^n U_i^{O_i(r)}$. Use the grid Alexander value for each state and assign filtration drop $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$ to this term.

Return the ordered state list, the mode and coefficient ring, the exact differential matrix obtained by summing coefficients modulo two, the state Maslov and Alexander values, and the filtration data for the full filtered mode. The algorithm returns this finite presentation only; its identification with knot Floer homology and its independence of the chosen grid are separate theorems. The factor $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ is not multiplied into the output.

For every one-component toroidal grid and each of the tilde, associated-graded minus, and full filtered minus modes, the differential defined by the grid-complex algorithm satisfies $\partial^2=0$ over its stated coefficient ring.

derivations.claim: Starting at the bottom-left $O$, the oriented route follows its row to the bottom-right $X$, then follows that column to the top-right $O$, then that row to the top-left $X$, then that column back to the starting $O$. Thus the link has one component. Its planar projection has no transverse self-intersection: the four segments meet only at these marked turning points, and smoothing the four corners gives a simple closed planar curve, which bounds a disk. Therefore it is an unknot. [F1, given, construct]

There are exactly two grid states, the two permutations of two columns. For either ordered pair of distinct states, the rectangles from the first state to the second are the bottom-left and top-right cells, each containing one $O$; the reverse rectangles are the bottom-right and top-left cells, each containing one $X$. No such rectangle is counted in tilde mode, and there are no rectangles from a state to itself. Hence the tilde differential is zero. [F1, F2, construct]

The tilde chain group has its two grid states as a basis, and its differential is zero by step 1.2. The chain condition is supplied by [F3], so its homology equals this two-dimensional chain group and has rank two. [F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

derivations.claim: The marking permutation sends the $O$ in row $0$ to the $X$ in column $1$ and then to the $O$ in row $1$; it continues from row $1$ through column $2$ to row $2$, and from row $2$ through column $0$ back to row $0$. Thus the grid has one component. In its planar projection the oriented path has vertices $(0.5,0.5),(1.5,0.5),(1.5,1.5),(2.5,1.5),(2.5,2.5),(0.5,2.5)$ and returns to $(0.5,0.5)$. These six axis-parallel edges form a simple polygon and meet only at consecutive endpoints, so the projection has no crossings and is an unknot diagram. [F1, given, construct]

The six grid states, in lexicographic order as row-to-column permutations, are $012,021,102,120,201,210$. The only cells containing neither marking are $(r,c)=(0,2),(1,0),(2,1)$; each is isolated from the other two by marked cells across every side, including the torus identifications. Every marking-free rectangle made of more than one cell contains a pair of side-adjacent cells and hence a marking. Therefore the only possible tilde rectangles are these three single-cell rectangles. [F1, F2, construct]

For state $201$, the SW and NE corners of cell $(r,c)=(0,2)$ lie in that state and the other two corners give state $021$; cell $(1,0)$ similarly gives $201\to210$, and cell $(2,1)$ gives $201\to102$, with the row interval in the last cell wrapping around the torus. No other state has the SW/NE pair of corners of any of these empty cells. Thus the differential matrix, with rows and columns ordered $012,021,102,120,201,210$ and rows indexing targets, has rows
$$000000,\quad 000010,\quad 000010,\quad 000000,\quad 000000,\quad 000010.$$

derivations.claim: Multiplication by $f=T+U$ commutes with $d$, because $d$ is $R$-linear and is extended coefficientwise in $T$. Consequently $D^2(a,b)=(0,df a+fd a)=(0,0)$. The first-copy degree shift makes both components of $D$ have Maslov degree $-1$; the cross component $fa$ preserves or lowers filtration, since $f$ lowers filtration by one and the first copy is already shifted down by one. Thus $B$ is the asserted filtered complex. [given, algebra]

Define $e:C[T]\to C$ by evaluation at $T=U$. Define the $R$-linear divided-difference map $q:C[T]\to C[T]$ by $q(c)=0$ on constant polynomials and $q(cT^r)=c\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}T^{r-1-t}U^t$ for $r\ge1$. Expanding the finite geometric sum gives $fq(p)=p+e(p)$, with $e(p)$ included as a constant polynomial. Also $e(fp)=0$ and hence $q(fp)=p$. The latter follows directly on monomials, or by cancellation in the displayed sum; it uses no division in $C$. [given, construct, algebra]

For the general variant write $d_0=d(U)$, extended coefficientwise to $E$, and $d(T)=d_0+f d_1(T)$ by entrywise polynomial division. Every entry of $d(T)-d_0$ vanishes at $T=U$ and is divisible by the monic polynomial $f=T+U$, so $d_1$ exists without coefficient denominators. Since $d(T)^2=0$, evaluation gives $d_0^2=0$; expanding the square and cancelling the injective scalar $f$ on the free module gives $d_0d_1+d_1d_0+f d_1^2=0$. [given, construct, algebra]

The maps $e,q$ commute with $d$ because their formulas apply to the polynomial variable $T$ alone and every coefficient of $d$ belongs to $R$. Let $P(a,b)=e(b)$ and $I(c)=(0,c)$. Then $PD=dP$ by $e(fa)=0$, $DI=I\circ d$, and $PI=\operatorname{id}_C$. Thus $P$ and $I$ are chain maps with composite identity on $C$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

Taking the ordinary scalar quotient $T=U$ sends $f$ to $0$. It sends $C[T]$ to $C$, not to a further homology group. Thus the quotient differential is $(a,b)\mapsto(da,db)$, with the unchanged first-copy shift. This is exactly $C\otimes V$. A further scalar quotient of the old coefficients commutes with this componentwise construction and yields the same formula for the quotient of $C$. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Use the maps $e,q$ of step 1.2 in the fixed basis of $E$, and put $P(a,b)=e(b)$, $I(c)=(d_1c,c)$ for $c$ in the quotient, included as a constant polynomial in this basis, and $H(a,b)=(q(b),0)$. The relation in step 1.3 gives $d(T)d_1=d_1d_0$, and hence $DI=I d_0$. Also $PD=d_0P$ and $PI=\operatorname{id}$. For an arbitrary $b$, the divided-difference identity gives $q(d(T)b)=d_0q(b)+d_1b$, whereas $d(T)q(b)=d_0q(b)+f d_1q(b)$. Their sum is $d_1e(b)$. It follows that $DH+HD=(a+d_1e(b),b+e(b))=\operatorname{id}+IP$. The component formulas also give $HI=PH=H^2=0$. Thus these are deformation-retraction identities for the general polynomial differential. [step 1.2, step 1.3, construct, algebra]

Set $H(a,b)=(q(b),0)$. The first components of $DH+HD$ sum to $dq(b)+q(db+fa)=a$, and the second component is $fq(b)=b+e(b)$. Thus $DH+HD=\operatorname{id}_B+IP$. Furthermore $HI=0$, $PH=0$, and $H^2=0$ by their component formulas. These identities give a chain deformation retraction, without any assertion that the evaluation map is linear over $R[T]$. It is linear over the required ring $R$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

Evaluation replaces powers of $T$ by the same powers of $U$ and therefore preserves the degrees and filtration. In $q(cT^r)$ each summand has one fewer variable factor than $cT^r$, so its Maslov degree rises by two and its filtration by one before placement in the first copy. The first-copy shift then makes $H$ have Maslov degree $+1$ and filtration degree $0$. Inclusion has degree and filtration degree zero. Consequently the retraction is filtered with precisely the asserted grading behavior. [step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra]

An actual chain homotopy equivalence over a polynomial ring remains one after any scalar quotient: tensor each chain map, homotopy, and homotopy identity with the new coefficient module. No flatness is required for this statement, since it is an equality of maps and homotopies, rather than a claim that tensor products commute with homology. Combining this observation with steps 3.1 and 2.2 proves the final comparison assertion. [step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra]

The matrix $d_1$ has Maslov degree $+1$, since division by $f$ removes degree $-2$ from $d$. Its filtration degree is at most $+1$: replacing a factor $T$ by $U$ preserves filtration, and divided difference removes exactly one variable factor from every monomial. Consequently the first component of $I$ after its downward shift has degree zero and does not increase filtration. The same degree calculation for $q$ as in step 4.1 applies to $H$. The general retraction is therefore filtered, not merely an unfiltered homology isomorphism. [step 4.1, step 1.3, step 2.3, algebra]

If the stated homotopy $L$ exists, the triangular map $J(a,b)=(a,b+La)$ is its own inverse. From $dL+Ld=f$ one computes $D_0J=JD_f$, where $D_0$ and $D_f$ are respectively the zero-map-cone and $f$-cone differentials. Its degree is zero: $La$ lies in the second copy and has the same degree and no larger filtration than $a$ in the shifted first copy. Thus $J$ is a filtered chain isomorphism from the $f$-cone to $E\otimes V$. Combining it with the retraction in step 2.3 yields the claimed filtered chain homotopy equivalence of the quotient. [step 2.3, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

After any earlier relation $T_i=U$ has been imposed, the remaining basis module is still free over the polynomial ring in the remaining independent variables. Tensoring the identity $dL+Ld=T+U$ with that coefficient quotient preserves it and its degree bounds. Apply the general quotient retraction and triangular cone isomorphism successively to each remaining variable. Each step contributes one copy of $V$, so $n-1$ relations contribute precisely $V^{\otimes(n-1)}$. The comparisons are over the surviving ring at each step and therefore over the chosen $\mathbb F_2[U]$ action at the end. [step 1.3, step 2.3, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

derivations.claim: Draw both diagrams on one torus with their markings fixed. Their horizontal circles agree, and all but one vertical circle agree. Denote the different vertical circles by $\beta,\gamma$; draw them crossing transversely at two points $a,b$ away from the horizontal circles, with one marking-bearing bigon on each side. The noninterleaving interval condition allows the two intervening annular regions to avoid all markings: draw $\gamma$ around the two endpoint levels of the exchanged columns, leaving each endpoint marking on its original side. Choose $a$ as the southern tip of the bigon with $\beta$ on its western boundary and $\gamma$ on its eastern boundary; the other tip is $b$. For a switch, the shared-row $O,X$ lie in the same straight-strip region but on opposite sides of the curved circles; the same marking-free intervening annuli remain. [given, construct]

For states $\mathbf x$ of $G$ and $\mathbf y'$ of $G'$, count embedded disks with five convex corners, four in $\mathbf x\cup\mathbf y'$ and the fifth at $a$, boundary on the combined circles, and horizontal boundary satisfying $\partial(\partial_\alpha p)=\mathbf y'-\mathbf x$. Require that the interior contains no state point, but impose no marking restriction. Define $P(\mathbf x)$ as the sum of the targets with coefficient $U^{O(p)}$. Define $Q$ in the reverse direction using the distinguished corner $b$. Define $H$ on $G$ by the same rule for six-sided embedded disks with four state corners and the other two corners $a,b$; define $H'$ on $G'$ in the same way. A side cannot travel completely around its circle in an embedded polygon, so there are finitely many possible sides, corners, and polygons. These are consequently finite polynomial-module maps. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

To compute their degrees, use the nearest-point correspondence from a $\gamma$ state to a $\beta$ state, replacing just its point on the changed circle. The connecting small triangle $t$ contains no other state coordinate. Expanding the pair-counting formula on the two diagrams gives $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf x')=-1+2n_O(t)$: the self-state terms are equal, the marking-self terms differ by $-1$, and the state-marking cross term differs by $0$ or $-2$ according to which side of the marked level the moved point lies. These are the four choices of side and direction of the triangle. Attaching $t$ on the available side of a pentagon yields a rectangle, so [F2] gives $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y')=-2n_O(p)$ and $A(\mathbf x)-A(\mathbf y')=n_X(p)-n_O(p)$ for an empty pentagon. For a hexagon, fill its missing bigon, which contains one $O$ and one $X$, to obtain a rectangle; [F2] then gives $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=-1-2n_O(h)$ and $A(\mathbf x)-A(\mathbf y)=n_X(h)-n_O(h)$. Thus the weighted pentagon maps have degree zero and filtration drop $n_X(p)$, and the weighted hexagon maps have degree $+1$ and filtration drop $n_X(h)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Expand $d'P+Pd$, keeping each composite domain and its multiplicities. When four coordinates of the initial state are absent from the terminal state, the rectangle and pentagon have disjoint sets of moving coordinates; commute their order, retaining their supports. This is an involution without fixed points, including when the supports overlap with local multiplicity two. When three coordinates move, cut the composite at its reflex corner in the two possible directions. For multiplicity-one domains this is the ordinary seven-corner region. If a multiplicity is two, the reflex corner is the distinguished corner $a$; following the two possible outgoing edges there again yields exactly the alternate rectangle-pentagon decomposition. Emptiness is preserved, since a forbidden state point in either alternative piece would lie in the interior of an original piece. Thus all these terms pair with the same total $O$-weight. [F1, F3, step 2.1, construct]

The remaining possibility in $d'P+Pd$ is that the endpoints differ only on the changed circle. A horizontal thin annulus with a small triangle removed has two decompositions and cancels internally. A vertical thin annulus together with that triangle has one decomposition. There are exactly two such vertical domains: adjoining the marking-free annulus on the western side of the changed circle, or adjoining the marking-free annulus on the eastern side. They have the same initial and terminal states; their difference is the difference of those two marking-free annuli. Their marking multiplicities and therefore their polynomial weights agree. They cancel with each other. These cases exhaust the compositions: the rectangle changes two coordinates and the pentagon changes the coordinate on the replaced circle together with at most one further coordinate, so the number of unmatched coordinates is four, three, or one. Hence $d'P+Pd=0$. Exchanging the roles of the two diagrams proves $dQ+Qd'=0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra]

Expand $dH+Hd+QP$ and group rectangle-hexagon, hexagon-rectangle, and pentagon-pentagon decompositions by domain. Four moving coordinates give the same commuting pair as in step 3.2. Three moving coordinates give eight-corner domains: either seven convex corners and one reflex corner, or five convex corners and three reflex corners, two of the latter at $a,b$. In the first case cut at the sole reflex corner in its two possible directions. In the second, at two reflex corners the outgoing cut is forced by the boundary orientation; at the remaining one either direction is allowed. The resulting two decompositions are exactly the alternative ordered polygon pairs, with equal weights. This also describes the pair when its two types differ, for example one rectangle-hexagon decomposition and one pentagon-pentagon decomposition. citations.quote: Let $G$ be a toroidal grid of grid number $n$ representing one oriented knot, and let $M_{\mathbb O}$, $M_{\mathbb X}$, and $A_G$ be the functions defined from its finite point sets and the pair-counting function $J$. Then $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integer-valued, and every rectangle $r$ from a grid state $\mathbf x$ to a grid state $\mathbf y$ satisfies $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$ and $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb X}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Consequently $A_G$ is integer-valued and $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing a knot, and use the three differentials defined by the grid-complex algorithm. For any fixed source and target states, every non-annular composite of two counted rectangles has exactly two ordered rectangle decompositions; the two decompositions have equal $O$-monomial weights and are either both counted or both excluded in each mode. Returning composites consist of thin annuli, one horizontal annulus for each row and one vertical annulus for each column. Every such annulus contains one $X$ and one $O$, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, each horizontal annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking, and each vertical annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking; every $O$-variable occurs once in each family and therefore twice in total. derivations.claim: Follow the alternating horizontal and vertical boundary segments of an incoming domain, starting at the component of $\mathbf x$ on the new vertical circle. At an ordinary corner, three zero adjacent coefficients force the next segment and its direction; there is no choice to add an annulus without violating this condition at a state corner. The first segment and the distinguished vertical circle cut off a unique empty rectangle. Removing it gives the next boundary segment; remove the next forced rectangle as well. These two removals reduce the complexity by two and the three common local multiplicities at $c$ by one. Continuing ends at the zero domain for left type or the southeast rectangle for right type. This proves by induction a factorization into $m-1$ empty rectangles for complexity $m$, unique among factorizations in which every rectangle has a side on the new vertical circle. It also proves that left type has odd complexity $2k+1$ and right type even complexity $2k+2$. Both are bounded by the number of state coordinates. Since the set of empty rectangles is finite, only finitely many such factorizations and incoming domains occur. [given, construct]

Let $d'$ be the differential of $G'$ and $d$ that of $G$. To compare $D d'$ with the cone differential followed by $D$, lift rectangles of $G$ to $G'$ using the deletion correspondence. There are five possible rectangle types: A avoids $c$ and is empty; B has $c$ at a corner and is empty; C has $c$ in the interior of a side and is empty; D contains the initial-state point $c$ in its interior and no other state point; E contains $c$ in its interior while its initial state does not contain $c$, and is empty. Rectangles in $G$ correspond to types A and D. Rectangles counted in $d'$ have types A, B, C, E. In the cone there are also invisible terms, from its first to second copy, with coefficient $U_1+U_2$. [given, construct]

Apply [F1] to these $m-1$ rectangles. For a domain $p$ ending at $\mathbf y$, omission of the $U_1$ power gives the changes $A(\mathbf x)-A(U^{O_{\ne1}(p)}\mathbf y)=n_X(p)-O_1(p)$ and $M(\mathbf x)-M(U^{O_{\ne1}(p)}\mathbf y)=m-1-2O_1(p)$. For left type, $O_1(p)=k$ and $X_2(p)=k$; for right type, $O_1(p)=k$ and $X_2(p)=k+1$. Deleting $c$ raises the degree and Alexander value of a state in $I$ by one: in the finite pair-count formula, the new state corner contributes a loss of one in $M_O$ and none in $M_X$, so the Alexander loss is one as well. Account also for the downward shift in the first cone summand. The weighted output then has the same Maslov degree as its input, and its filtration drop is exactly $X_1(p)+X_3(p)+\cdots$, a nonnegative integer. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

Classify a composition of an incoming domain of complexity $m$ and a rectangle by the rectangle type and number of common moving corners. The possible types are (A-0), (A-1), (A-2), (A-3); (B-0), (B-3), (B-4); (C-1); (D-0), (D-1); and the invisible type I. Here (B-0) has $m=1$, (B-3) has $m=3$, (B-4) has $m=2$; (A-2) requires $m\ge4$, (A-3) requires $m\ge3$, and (C-1),(D-1) require $m\ge2$. These are exhaustive: at an ordinary corner the three zero coefficients force the outgoing rectangle edge; counting its endpoints leaves precisely the listed numbers of common corners. A rectangle of type E cannot be followed by an incoming domain: following the latter's forced boundary from the new vertical circle would put either an initial-state point inside that rectangle or a terminal-state point in the incoming domain. The only extra edge in a type-D composition is the state point $c$, giving (D-0) or (D-1). [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

Among (A-3) compositions, those wrapping through the horizontal row of $O_2$ are exceptional; those wrapping vertically through $O_1$ or horizontally through the row of $O_1$ are ordinary. Among (C-1) compositions, the exceptional case is a preceding rectangle containing both $X_1,O_1$ and an incoming domain of even complexity; the other two cases contain $X_1$ alone, or contain $X_2$ alone with odd complexity. Among (D-1) compositions, wrapping through the row of $O_2$ is exceptional; wrapping through $O_1$ is ordinary. Let $\delta$ be the incoming domain's innermost height for the cases involving $X_2$ or both $X_1,O_1$, and its innermost width for the case containing $X_1$ alone. Thus $\delta$ is a positive number of row or column strips. This specifies all subcases without imposing an $X$ exclusion. [step 2.2, construct]

Contributions of (A-0) cancel by commuting their disjoint boundary changes. Contributions of (A-1) cancel by cutting at the unique ordinary reflex corner in its two directions. The two resulting domain decompositions have the same total multiplicities, hence the same monomial. An (A-2) composition of incoming complexity $m+2$ cancels with (D-0) of complexity $m>1$: slide the cut through the two consecutive boundary segments next to $c$, thereby moving the state point $c$ from a counted incoming domain into the lifted rectangle's interior. The same slide for (D-0) of complexity one yields (B-3) of complexity three. These are inverse cut operations, so every contribution in these classes appears once in its indicated pair. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, construct]

The two (B-4) domains are the vertical thin annulus through $O_1,X_2$ and horizontal thin annulus through $O_2,X_2$. Their weights are respectively $U_1$ and $U_2$, since in this case the rectangle, rather than the incoming domain, carries that variable. Their sum cancels the invisible term applied to the zero incoming domain. A (B-0) rectangle ending at $c$ cancels with an ordinary (A-3) composition of complexity three: adjoin the row or column annulus through $O_1$ according as $c$ is the rectangle's upper-left or lower-right corner, and cut at the other two corners. This operation inserts two extra boundary segments and reverses when that annulus is removed. The added $O_1$ multiplicity lies in the incoming part, whose weight omits $U_1$, so the coefficients agree. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

For an ordinary (C-1) composition $r*p$ containing $X_2$, adjoin the horizontal thin annulus through $O_1$; for the case containing $X_1$ alone, adjoin the vertical thin annulus through $O_1$. If $\delta=1$, the forced alternative cut is (D-1) of the same incoming complexity; if $\delta>1$, it is ordinary (A-3) with complexity greater by two. In both cases the alternative domain has exactly one contributing cut: its location is forced by the first state point in the added strip. Removing the strip recovers $r*p$, so these cancellations are bijections. Again the added annulus changes only the omitted $O_1$ exponent in the incoming part. Therefore each pair has equal coefficient. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

For an exceptional (C-1) composition of even complexity $2k$, the composite itself is an incoming left domain of complexity $2k+1$ and gives an invisible contribution. Adjoin the horizontal thin annulus through $O_2$ and use the forced alternative cut. If $\delta=1$, that cut has type exceptional (D-1) and complexity $2k$; if $\delta>1$, it has type exceptional (A-3) and complexity $2k+2$. The (C-1) rectangle contributes an additional $U_1$ because it contains $O_1$; the annulus-added alternative contributes an additional $U_2$; the invisible term contributes $U_1+U_2$. The remaining monomial is common to all three, so their total vanishes. Removing the added strip or viewing the invisible incoming domain with its first cut recovers the same triple, with no duplication. This exhausts exceptional (D-1), exceptional (A-3) and invisible terms of complexity greater than one. Together with the preceding cancellation cases, every term in $D d'+d_{\mathrm{cone}}D$ has cancelled. Thus $D$ is a chain map. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

By step 2.1, the associated-graded map retains just domains avoiding $X_1,X_3,\ldots$. The northwest cell contains $X_1$ and has local multiplicity $k$ in either nontrivial type. Avoiding $X_1$ therefore forces $k=0$. Left type would then have southwest multiplicity $-1$, so its only surviving term is the separately allowed zero domain. Right type with $k=0$ has complexity two and the forced factorization has one rectangle. Thus the surviving domains have complexity one or two. The complexity-one term deletes $c$ from a state in $I$; complexity two is precisely an empty rectangle through $X_2$ ending in $I$, with no other $X$, weighted by its $O$-monomial. This is the stated associated-graded map. Finiteness and grading were proved above, and the full chain-map identity was proved in step 5.1. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

derivations.claim: The operator $N=\Delta h_0$ has Maslov degree zero and strictly lowers Alexander degree. If an input has Maslov degree $j$ and Alexander degree at most $a$, then $N^r$ of that input has Alexander degree at most $a-r$. Below the finite lower bound for degree $j$ it must vanish. The sum defines a module-linear map because every summand is module-linear and, for each fixed finite set of inputs and their sum, one can take a common finite truncation. From $\delta^2=\delta_0^2=0$ obtain $\delta_0\Delta+\Delta\delta_0+\Delta^2=0$. Let $G'$ be an $X$ stabilization of type southwest of a knot grid $G$. In the four cells incident to the new crossing $c$, the northwest cell contains $X_1$, the northeast cell contains the new $O_1$, the southeast cell contains $X_2$, and the southwest cell is empty. Let $O_2$ be the old $O$ in the row of $X_2$. Write $I$ for states containing $c$, and identify such a state $\mathbf y$ with $e(\mathbf y)=\mathbf y\setminus\{c\}$ in $G$. Retain the independent variables of all markings.

An incoming left domain is either the zero domain or a nonnegative domain from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y\in I$ with the following properties. At every state corner other than $c$, at least three adjacent cell multiplicities vanish; near $c$, three multiplicities equal $k$ and the southwest multiplicity is $k-1$; exactly $2k+1$ coordinates of $\mathbf y$ are absent from $\mathbf x$. For an incoming right domain, replace the southwest exception by southeast multiplicity $k+1$, and the number of absent coordinates by $2k+2$; the zero domain is not of right type. Denote these sets by $\pi^{iL},\pi^{iR}$. Define $D^{iL},D^{iR}$ by counting their targets $e(\mathbf y)$, with weight $\prod_{j\ne1}U_j^{O_j(p)}$, omitting the power of the new variable. Then
$$D=(D^{iL},D^{iR}):C^-(G')\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cone}(U_1+U_2:C^-(G)[U_1]\to C^-(G)[U_1])$$
is a finite polynomial-module chain map preserving Maslov degree and not increasing Alexander filtration. The first cone summand is shifted down by one in both degree and filtration. Its associated-graded map counts only domains avoiding $X_1,X_3,\ldots$; these have complexity at most two and give exactly the usual graded destabilization map: deletion of $c$ on $I$ in the first component, and rectangles through $X_2$ on the other states in the second component.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing a knot, and use the three differentials defined by the grid-complex algorithm. For any fixed source and target states, every non-annular composite of two counted rectangles has exactly two ordered rectangle decompositions; the two decompositions have equal $O$-monomial weights and are either both counted or both excluded in each mode. Returning composites consist of thin annuli, one horizontal annulus for each row and one vertical annulus for each column. Every such annulus contains one $X$ and one $O$, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, each horizontal annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking, and each vertical annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking; every $O$-variable occurs once in each family and therefore twice in total. Thus all returning terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Every counted rectangle term has Maslov degree $-1$ and lowers Alexander filtration by exactly the number of $X$-markings in its interior; the modes excluding $X$ preserve Alexander grading.

For every one-component toroidal grid and each of the tilde, associated-graded minus, and full filtered minus modes, the differential defined by the grid-complex algorithm satisfies $\partial^2=0$ over its stated coefficient ring.

Work over a polynomial ring of characteristic two, with an integer Maslov grading and integer Alexander filtration. Let $E$ be a based module whose homogeneous piece of each Maslov degree is finite dimensional over the coefficient field and has finite upper and lower Alexander bounds. Let $\delta_0,\delta$ be two module-linear differentials of Maslov degree $-1$ on $E$, where $\delta_0$ preserves Alexander degree and $\Delta=\delta-\delta_0$ strictly lowers it. Suppose a module-linear map $h_0$ of Maslov degree $+1$ preserves Alexander degree and satisfies $\delta_0h_0+h_0\delta_0=\operatorname{id}$. Then
$$h=h_0\sum_{r\ge0}(\Delta h_0)^r$$
is a well-defined filtered module-linear contraction for $\delta$, so $\delta h+h\delta=\operatorname{id}$. The sum is finite on each input. If $E$ has a finite module basis and each map in the formula is a finite polynomial matrix, the sum is a finite polynomial matrix as well.

In particular, for a filtered degree-zero chain map $F:C\to B$, any explicit Alexander-degree-preserving contraction of the cone of its associated-graded map lifts by this formula to a contraction of the cone of $F$, provided the stated degreewise bounds hold. The upper-right block of the lifted contraction is a filtered chain homotopy inverse to $F$, and its diagonal blocks give homotopies from both composites to the identity. If the initial data are finite domain counts, these matrices are finite sums of compositions of those domain counts.

Let $R=\mathbb F_2[U,Z_1,\ldots,Z_s]$, and let $(C,d)$ be a graded, Alexander-filtered chain complex of free $R$-modules. Every variable has Maslov degree $-2$ and Alexander filtration degree $-1$, and $d$ has Maslov degree $-1$ and does not increase filtration. Extend scalars to $C[T]$, with $T$ having the same degrees. Put $f=T+U$ and form the cone $B=C[T]^{\mathrm{low}}\oplus C[T]$, with differential $D(a,b)=(da,db+fa)$; the first copy is shifted down by one in both Maslov degree and filtration. Regarded over $R$, this cone has an explicit filtered chain deformation retraction onto $C$. Its projection is evaluation of the second component at $T=U$, its inclusion is $c\mapsto(0,c)$, and its homotopy is polynomial divided difference in the second component, placed in the first component.

In contrast, the ordinary scalar quotient $T=U$ taken before homology gives the zero-map cone $C\oplus C^{\mathrm{low}}$, equivalently $C\otimes V$, where $V$ has zero differential and bidegrees $(0,0)$ and $(-1,-1)$. Any further ordinary quotient of the old variables has the same direct-sum description with the corresponding quotient of $C$. Thus an equivalence of a basepoint insertion complex with this cone over the full polynomial ring implies invariance for the chosen single-variable action and an extra $V$ factor after simultaneous collapse. These are different operations.

More generally, let $E$ be free over $R[T]$ on a homogeneous filtered basis, and let its differential $d(T)$ have the same degree and filtration behavior, with polynomial matrix entries. Then $\operatorname{Cone}(T+U:E\to E)$ admits an explicit filtered deformation retraction over $R$ onto the ordinary quotient $(E/(T+U)E,d(U))$. If multiplication by $T+U$ on $E$ has a polynomial-linear homotopy $L$ with $dL+Ld=T+U$, Maslov degree $-1$, and filtration degree at most $-1$, this quotient is filtered chain homotopy equivalent over $R$ to $E\otimes V$. Iterating applies to independent marking variables and survives every earlier scalar quotient. Thus pairwise such homotopies imply that simultaneous collapse of $n$ variables to one has type $E\otimes V^{\otimes(n-1)}$ over the chosen variable action.

derivations.claim: For the associated-graded differential, $N$ is a subcomplex: a rectangle from $N$ to $I$ necessarily crosses $X_1$ or $X_2$, as its two sides terminating at $c$ surround one of the two adjacent $X$ cells. Thus the graded stabilized complex has differential $(d_I a,d_N b+\alpha a)$ on $I\oplus N$. Deleting $c$ identifies $(I,d_I)$ with the smaller associated-graded complex shifted down by one in both gradings; rectangles avoiding $X$ correspond under this deletion and cannot contain $O_1$. Let $B$ denote the smaller complex with the new polynomial variable adjoined and without that shift. [F1, F3, given, construct]

Define $p:N\to B$ by counting rectangles ending in $I$ and containing $X_2$ and no other $X$, then deleting $c$, with all $O$ powers included. Define $i:B\to N$ by adjoining $c$ and counting rectangles containing $O_1$ and no $X$, omitting the $U_1$ power. Define $k:N\to N$ by rectangles containing both $O_1,X_2$ and no other $X$, again omitting $U_1$. The same grading changes as in [F1] make $p,i$ degree zero and $k$ degree $(1,0)$. For $d_Bp+pd_N$, a nonreturning domain has its two alternative cuts from [F2], with the unique selected $X_2$ in either cut; there are no returning domains between the disjoint endpoint sets $N,I$. Hence $p$ is a chain map. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

The composition $pi$ counts pairs of rectangles joining $I$ back to $I$, with one through $O_1$ and the other through $X_2$. The marked-cell positions and the state point $c$ force their union to be the thin vertical annulus through those two cells. For each input state it has one permissible cut; no other state point lies inside its pieces. The omitted $U_1$ power leaves weight one. Therefore $pi=1$. In $ip+d_Nk+kd_N$, nonreturning domains have the alternative two cuts from [F2], preserving their selected marked multiplicities, and cancel. Returning domains must contain both $O_1$ and $X_2$, so the same vertical thin annulus is the only possibility. For an input in $N$, its unique cut places it in exactly one of the three summands according to the positions of its points on the two boundary circles. Its weight is again one. Hence $ip+d_Nk+kd_N=1_N$. Since $p$ is a chain map, commuting the last identity with $d_N$ gives $(d_Ni+id_B)p=0$; right-composition with $i$ and $pi=1$ proves that $i$ is a chain map as well. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Put $P_N=1+ip$ and $k'=P_NkP_N$. These are explicit finite polynomial matrices. Since $pi=1$, $P_N$ is an idempotent chain map, $pk'=0$, and $k'i=0$. The identity in step 3.1 implies $d_Nk'+k'd_N=P_N$. In the first coordinate of [F1]'s graded target, use the identification of $I$ with the shifted copy of $B$. Under this identification, $D_0(a,b)=(a,pb)$, and its target has cone differential $(d_Ia,d_B b+fa)$ with $f=U_1+U_2$. The chain-map identity already proved in [F1] gives $p\alpha=f$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Define $S_0(a,b)=(a,ib+k'\alpha a)$ and $K_0(a,b)=(0,k'b)$. Direct matrix multiplication, using $p\alpha=f$ and $d_Nk'+k'd_N=1+ip$, gives $d_{G',0}S_0=S_0d_{\mathrm{cone},0}$, $D_0S_0=1$, and $S_0D_0+1=d_{G',0}K_0+K_0d_{G',0}$. Also $D_0K_0=0$. Every map has the degrees required of a graded equivalence or homotopy: $\alpha$ lowers Maslov degree by one and has filtration degree zero, and $k'$ has degree $(1,0)$. Thus this is an explicit associated-graded contraction. [step 4.1, construct, algebra]

On the cone of $D_0$, whose underlying module is $C_{G',0}[1]\oplus B_{\mathrm{cone},0}$, define $h_0(c,b)=(K_0c+S_0b,0)$. The identities in step 5.1 give $\delta_0h_0+h_0\delta_0=1$: its first component is $(dK_0+K_0d+S_0D_0)c=c$, with the terms in $b$ cancelling because $S_0$ is a chain map; its second component is $D_0K_0c+D_0S_0b=b$. This is the explicit Alexander-preserving cone contraction to which [F4] applies. [step 5.1, construct, algebra]

Use the same bases for the actual filtered cone of $D$. Its differential is $\delta_0+\Delta$, with $\Delta$ strictly lowering Alexander degree, by [F1] and the rectangle filtration formula. Each variable has Maslov degree $-2$ and there are finitely many state and cone generators. In a fixed Maslov degree, only finitely many monomials can occur: their total exponent is fixed by the degree of their basis generator. Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing one oriented knot, and let $\partial^-$ be the full filtered minus differential over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_n]$. Call $O_i$ and $O_j$ consecutive when the $X$-marking in the row of $O_i$ lies in the column of $O_j$. Let $X_\ell$ be that marking and define the module map
$$H_\ell(\mathbf x)=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{r\in\operatorname{Rect}^{\circ}(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\\X_\ell\in\operatorname{Int}(r)}}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}U_a^{O_a(r)}\right)\mathbf y.$$
Then $\partial^-H_\ell+H_\ell\partial^-=(U_i+U_j)\operatorname{id}$. The map $H_\ell$ has Maslov degree $-1$ and does not raise the Alexander filtration. Consequently multiplication by any two variables $U_i,U_j$ is filtered chain homotopic, since the consecutive relation follows the single cycle of the knot grid.

Let $G$ be a toroidal grid representing a knot, and use the three differentials defined by the grid-complex algorithm. For any fixed source and target states, every non-annular composite of two counted rectangles has exactly two ordered rectangle decompositions; the two decompositions have equal $O$-monomial weights and are either both counted or both excluded in each mode. Returning composites consist of thin annuli, one horizontal annulus for each row and one vertical annulus for each column. Every such annulus contains one $X$ and one $O$, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode, each horizontal annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking, and each vertical annulus contributes the variable of its unique $O$-marking; every $O$-variable occurs once in each family and therefore twice in total. Thus all returning terms cancel over $\mathbb F_2$. Every counted rectangle term has Maslov degree $-1$ and lowers Alexander filtration by exactly the number of $X$-markings in its interior; the modes excluding $X$ preserve Alexander grading.

Let $D,D'$ be regular oriented link diagrams
([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]), regarded as decorated immersed oriented
$4$-valent planar graphs. Then $D$ and $D'$ are **planar isotopic** when there
is an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy
$\Phi\colon\mathbb R^2\times I\to\mathbb R^2$, with $\Phi_0=\mathrm{id}$ and
each $\Phi_t$ an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism
([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]), such that
$\Phi_1$ carries the decorated graph of $D$ to that of $D'$: it maps the image
curve of $D$ bijectively onto that of $D'$, carries the over/under datum of
every double point to the over/under datum of the corresponding double point,
and preserves the strand orientations. A **planar isotopy of diagrams** is a
family $D_t=\Phi_t(D_0)$ for such a jointly smooth ambient isotopy $\Phi$,
with the decorations transported by $\Phi_t$. The source curves are immersed,
not embedded in the plane at their crossings.

Planar isotopies are admitted as moves in the Reidemeister theorem: they carry
a regular projection between the exceptional times of a general-position
isotopy of the link, and no crossing of the diagram is created or destroyed
along them. They are listed separately from the three local moves
([[def-oriented-reidemeister-moves]]), of which R1 and R2 create or destroy crossings, while R3 rearranges three
existing crossings and preserves their number.
Composing planar isotopies and composing them with the local moves gives the
equivalence relation generated by the moves, and every single move below is
understood up to planar isotopy outside its small disk.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth and let $Z\subseteq N$ be an embedded submanifold
of codimension $c$, and suppose $F\pitchfork Z$. If $c\le m$, then
$F^{-1}(Z)$ is an embedded submanifold of $M$ of codimension $c$ (possibly empty). If $c>m$,
then $F^{-1}(Z)=\varnothing$. In the first case, for each $p\in F^{-1}(Z)$,

$$ T_pF^{-1}(Z)=\{v\in T_pM:dF_p(v)\in T_{F(p)}Z\}. $$

Near every crossing, two transverse branches determine its unique continued crossing; outside disjoint such disks, compact separated embedded edges have a positive separation. Thus a uniformly sufficiently small smooth perturbation stays regular with the same crossing incidence and decorations. Straightening the crossings and extending edge motions in their thin normal neighborhoods gives a planar isotopy locally in time; finitely many time neighborhoods cover the interval. Therefore such a perturbed family retains the asserted planar class. [F1, given, construct]

Embed the source circles times the interval in Euclidean space, and perturb both target coordinates by all ambient-coordinate monomials of degree at most $59$, times a smooth time cutoff zero on the fixed collars and positive elsewhere. At any at most eight distinct interior source points, this finite family independently controls intrinsic jets through order three: for a point $P_i$ multiply a degree-three Taylor polynomial by $\prod_{j\ne i}|P-P_j|^8$. Its degree is at most $3+8\cdot7=59$, its jets through order three vanish at every other selected point, and at $P_i$ the nonzero factor allows arbitrary prescribed jets by finite Taylor division. Intrinsic jets extend to ambient jets in the source's local product coordinates. The nonzero cutoff is invertible on jets. Keep the parameter ball small enough for step 1.1. Consequently [F2] applies to every smooth jet stratum listed below, on countably many coordinate pieces. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The remaining height coincidences have the following independent equations on distinct source points. Two critical points: $Y_x(x)=Y_x(y)=0$ and $Y(x)=Y(y)$, three equations on $(x,y,t)$. A critical point and a crossing: $Y_x(x)=0$, $g(y)=g(z)$, $Y(x)=Y(y)$, four equations on $(x,y,z,t)$. Two crossings: $g(x)=g(y)$, $g(z)=g(w)$, $Y(x)=Y(z)$, five equations on $(x,y,z,w,t)$. Time is common in each display. Transversality makes each coincidence isolated and makes its relative height derivative nonzero along the already continued special points; thus their order exchanges. Overlapping configurations either describe the same event with different orderings of its preimages, or force one of the extra conditions already excluded: a degenerate crossing-critical point, three special points of one height, a triple crossing, or a higher critical degeneracy. Take unordered crossing pairs and unordered pairs of special points to count an event once. The finitely many event types and their countably many coordinate pieces have a countable union of null exceptional parameter sets by [F2]; countable choice suffices for that union. Choose a parameter outside it in the prescribed small ball. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

It remains to justify finiteness despite deleted configuration diagonals. Critical degeneracies are a closed isolated subset of the compact source away from the fixed end collars, hence finite. Projected immersion gives a uniformly monotone projected coordinate on neighborhoods of every source point, so distinct crossing preimages stay uniformly separated; crossings cannot accumulate on that diagonal. Two merging critical points can occur only near a birth/death. Here is the needed critical-value separation without an unproved cubic normal-form premise. The preceding critical-point coordinate calculation, or the scalar implicit equation after scaling $x=vq$, gives $x_\pm=\pm v+O(v^2)$. Taylor expansion gives $Y_x(x,t)=at+bx^2/2+O(|x|^3+|xt|+t^2)$. Between them the bridge conditions hold by construction; the orientations and decorations were retained by step 1.1. This proves the claim. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

A bridge diagram is a smooth regular oriented planar link diagram with nondegenerate height-critical points, distinct heights for all critical points and crossings, and no height-critical crossing preimages. A bridge isotopy is a smooth family of bridge diagrams. A bridge-like rectangular diagram is nonempty and has vertical-over-horizontal crossings, distinct horizontal levels and distinct vertical abscissae; each horizontal segment is either a local maximum or minimum without crossings, or is height-monotone after smoothing and contains exactly one crossing. Smoothing means tilting each crossing-containing horizontal segment slightly in the direction of height travel and rounding corners in disjoint small neighborhoods, retaining all crossings and their decorations.

Every nonempty bridge diagram admits a bridge-like rectangular diagram whose smoothing is bridge isotopic to it. Any two bridge-like rectangular diagrams with bridge-isotopic smoothings give grids related by finitely many legal column commutations, after replacing their ordered levels and abscissae by consecutive grid coordinates. The short-column commutations only select this empty gap and do not change any old-column order, so this proof covers their whole composite. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, cases]

Let $s_A,s_B\in\{+1,-1\}$ record whether the other endpoint of column $A$, respectively $B$, is above or below $H$. An **oriented Reidemeister move** is one of the following local replacements of
a regular oriented link diagram ([[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]]),
performed inside a small closed disk while the diagram outside the disk is left
unchanged, and understood up to planar isotopy outside the disk
([[def-planar-isotopy-of-link-diagrams]]). All sign and orientation variants of
each local picture are included.

**(R1) Kink creation and deletion.** A single strand is replaced by a small
kink: two arcs crossing once and otherwise disjoint from the strand, with the
over/under datum of the new crossing as in the picture. The move is allowed in
both directions (create or delete the kink) and with both signs of the kink,
the sign being the sign of the crossing created. The orientations of the two
strands of the kink are the two possible consistent orientations through the
crossing, and all of them occur in the move list.

**(R2) Slide of two strands.** Two local arcs belonging to two strands are
replaced so that the number of crossings between those strands changes by two
of opposite signs: the standard picture slides one strand over or under the
other, creating or deleting the pair of crossings, with the two crossings being
the two possible signs in either order. All four orientation patterns of the
two strands at the two crossings are included.

**(R3) Sliding a strand past a crossing.** One strand is moved across an
existing crossing of two other strands, so that the crossing of the two other
strands passes from one side of the moving strand to the other; the three
crossings of the local picture keep their signs and the over/under data are
preserved. The three strands must have a consistent strict height order:
one is above both others, one below both, and the remaining strand is between
them. The cyclic over/under pattern is excluded. Every orientation pattern
and all six height orders of this standard local picture are included.

A local R2 or R3 picture is **braid-like** when, after a local coordinate
change and deformation, all participating strands run in the same positive
longitudinal direction. This is a local condition and does not require a
globally chosen braid axis. R1 is kept as a separate kink move.

The strands keep their orientations throughout every move. The union of the
three move types, together with planar isotopy, generates the equivalence
relation on diagrams used in the Reidemeister equivalence theorem below; the
moves are sometimes called R1, R2, R3 as above. Since every move changes the
diagram only inside a disk, it has a type and a finite list of local
orientation/sign variants, and each variant is realized by an ambient isotopy
as the next items show. The complete list of variants is required because the
Markov and Alexander constructions below act on oriented diagrams and count
signed crossings.

Thus no allowed height-order or local endpoint-order case is excluded. The cyclic over/under pattern would have no top arc and is not an R3 in [F2]. [F1, F2, step 1.3, step 2.3, construct, cases]
