A bridge-like rectangular diagram is nonempty and has vertical-over-horizontal crossings, distinct horizontal levels and distinct vertical abscissae; each horizontal segment is either a local maximum or minimum without crossings, or is height-monotone after smoothing and contains exactly one crossing. Smoothing means tilting each crossing-containing horizontal segment slightly in the direction of height travel and rounding corners in disjoint small neighborhoods, retaining all crossings and their decorations.

Every nonempty bridge diagram admits a bridge-like rectangular diagram whose smoothing is bridge isotopic to it. Any two bridge-like rectangular diagrams with bridge-isotopic smoothings give grids related by finitely many legal column commutations, after replacing their ordered levels and abscissae by consecutive grid coordinates. In particular this construction is independent, up to grid commutations, of every coordinate choice. The orientations determine the alternating $O,X$ markings by the row $O$-to-$X$ and column $X$-to-$O$ convention of the grid-diagram definition.

derivations.claim: Associate pieces to a jog-marked bridge diagram by cutting at extrema, undercrossing preimages and the distinguished regular points, leaving each overcrossing branch uncut. Every resulting piece is strictly height-monotone and has a nondegenerate closed height interval. At a critical or crossing height use its ordinary local cap or crossing order. At a distinguished regular height its two incident pieces lie consecutively among the local vertical pieces; prescribe their order by the side datum. This prescription is consistent with all other pieces: the distinguished point has a small disk disjoint from every other branch, and both incident vertical positions can be placed arbitrarily close to its original position on the selected sides. Pieces whose closed height intervals overlap have one prescribed left-to-right inequality, given by the graph order on an interior regular height or by this endpoint prescription. For every set of intervals containing a common height, these inequalities give a coherent total order. [given, construct]

The inequalities have no directed cycle. Three pairwise intersecting closed intervals have a common point, by comparing their largest left endpoint with their smallest right endpoint, so a triangle has coherent order. An interval intersection graph has no chordless cycle of length at least four: at a vertex with largest left endpoint both neighbors contain that endpoint and hence intersect each other. A chord of a shortest directed cycle, in either direction, would shorten it. Thus there is no directed cycle. Repeated removal of a vertex with no incoming edge gives a total order extending all inequalities, and assigning distinct increasing coordinates realizes them. At a critical height its horizontal join is an empty cap; at a crossing height the join meets exactly the overpassing piece; at a jog height its incident endpoints are consecutive and its join is empty and monotone. This constructs generalized rectifications with the stipulated incidence and side data. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The coordinate solution set is the open convex set defined by those strict inequalities. The special and distinguished height order is fixed in a bridge isotopy; pieces and their local orders continue without alteration. Hence two generalized rectifications of the same marked bridge class give two points of this same convex set after identifying pieces. Join them by a piecewise linear path which crosses each coordinate-equality hyperplane transversely and one at a time: choose an intermediate point in a small open ball avoiding the finitely many affine hyperplanes that force parallel or simultaneous crossings. Finitely many proper affine hyperplanes cannot cover an open ball, as their defining polynomial product is nonzero on some line segment. Only pieces with disjoint closed height intervals can meet in coordinate along this path, since intersecting intervals have a fixed strict inequality. At such a meeting the two columns are adjacent. The normalized grids therefore differ by a finite sequence of disjoint-interval column commutations. Ordered changes of height coordinates alter no normalized grid. This proves the uniqueness assertion, including closed interval endpoints at the distinguished heights. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

We also verify the bridge interpretation used here. On each interval of regular heights all pieces are ordered graphs, so ordered rectangular replacements have the same graph order. At a jog the replacement can be smoothed as a strictly height-monotone arc, with the same unique graph on each nearby horizontal fiber. At a crossing the difference of the two graph abscissae has a simple zero, so the positive affine horizontal map matching the two graph values extends smoothly over that zero by division by their simple vanishing factor. At a cap choose the small central smoothing as an affine horizontal image of the original Morse cap, and connect to its vertical legs by monotone branches in an empty neighborhood. Between these finitely many special neighborhoods extend the prescribed horizontal maps by positive derivatives on each gap: choose short end collars matching the prescribed derivatives, then a nonnegative interior bump whose integral fills the required positive image gap. Compact regular subbands give positive separation bounds. Smooth partitions in the height coordinate patch these maps by convex combinations, preserving positive horizontal derivative and all matching values. Outside a large rectangle take the identity. Interpolating the resulting increasing horizontal fiber maps with the identity, and separately interpolating increasing height reparameterizations, gives plane diffeomorphisms throughout. They prove the required bridge isotopies. The regular-jog case adds no singularity or critical point to this construction. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

The stated insertion is an actual marked stabilization. With $J>L$ and $Q>P$, the new block has $a$ northwest and southeast, $\bar a$ northeast and empty southwest. Row $L$ keeps its exterior $\bar a$, column $P$ keeps its exterior $\bar a$ at $T$, and the new row and column have one marking of each type. The new row interval is $[P,Q]$. Since these columns are adjacent, each old intervening row between $L,T$ has its endpoints outside that interval: its endpoints cannot be on $P$ except in rows $L,T$, and cannot be on the new $Q$. It is thus disjoint from $[P,Q]$ or strictly contains it. Commute $J$ upward one neighboring row at a time to the desired gap. No swap with $L,T$ is needed. Every exchange is legal. In that gap the new horizontal segment has one incident vertical leg above and one below, and crosses no old column, so it is a regular jog. Old crossing and critical height orders are unchanged. Its smoothing is bridge isotopic to the original after forgetting the distinguished point, by the local monotone-graph construction of step 3.2. [F1, given, construct, cases]

If the lower incident piece is to be on the left, insert $Q$ immediately left of $P$ instead. Use the same marks $(P,J,a),(Q,J,\bar a),(Q,L,a)$ and remove $(P,L,a)$. The new block now has $\bar a$ northwest, $a$ northeast and southwest, and empty southeast; it is again an allowed stabilization. The same adjacent-column interval argument moves the new row to the chosen height. Reflection here specifies a second finite recipe; no move from a grid to its reflection is assumed. Either type $a$ works by [F1]. Repeating these finite constructions inserts any finite ordered list of regular jogs and side data on the monotone pieces of an ordinary bridge rectification. An already inserted jog merely subdivides a piece; the next chosen regular point lies in one of its still vertical subpieces, to which the same construction applies. [F1, step 4.1, construct, cases]

Finally take a generalized bridge rectification $G$ and let $D$ be its jog-marked smoothing. Forget the regular points and choose an ordinary bridge rectification $B$ by [F2]. The distinguished points of $D$ lie on its monotone pieces at heights different from all special heights, so the two insertion recipes insert their matching ordered points and side data into $B$, giving a generalized grid $B'$. Steps 1.1–3.2 identify $B'$ and $G$ by disjoint-interval column commutations. Reverse those insertions to obtain a finite grid-move sequence from $G$ to $B$. This is an explicit reduction through fixed marked bridge data, not an appeal to planar invariance of an unproved global assignment. It proves every assertion. [F2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

Assume countable choice. In a nonempty generic marked rectangular diagram call a horizontal segment a cap if its two incident vertical segments extend to the same side in height, and monotone otherwise. A generalized bridge rectification has three kinds of horizontal segment: an empty cap, a monotone segment with exactly one crossing, and an empty monotone segment, called a regular jog. Smooth the first two kinds as in a bridge-like grid and tilt and round each regular jog monotonically in height. This produces a bridge diagram with one distinguished regular point for each jog, at pairwise distinct heights different from all critical and crossing heights. For a jog remember also whether its lower incident vertical piece is to the left or to the right of its upper incident piece. This is its side datum.

Two generalized bridge rectifications whose smoothed diagrams with distinguished points are bridge isotopic, with the same side data, are connected by finitely many disjoint-interval column commutations after normalization of coordinate orders. Every generalized bridge rectification is related by finite grid stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations to an ordinary bridge-like grid whose smoothing has the same bridge-isotopy class after forgetting the distinguished regular points.

More explicitly, a vertical grid piece in column $P$ from a mark $a$ at lower row $L$ to its complementary mark at upper row $T$ may be split at any regular height $L<h<T$. Insert $Q$ immediately right of $P$ and $J$ immediately above $L$, replace $(P,L,a)$ by $(P,J,a),(Q,J,\bar a),(Q,L,a)$, and commute the short row $J$ to the gap containing $h$. Here $\bar a$ is the other marking type. This inserts a crossing-free jog with the lower piece on the right. Insertion to the left gives the other side. These constructions, their inverses, and the preceding uniqueness assertion do not use global grid-isotopy generation.

A legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. A stabilization replaces a marking by a three-mark two-by-two block with its type twice at opposite corners, the complementary type once, and one empty corner, preserving one of each type per row and column.

Use planar grid markings with horizontal orientation from $O$ to $X$,
vertical orientation from $X$ to $O$, and vertical segments over horizontal
segments. An allowed commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns when
their closed marking intervals are disjoint or one is contained in the
interior of the other. A stabilization splits a row and column through a
chosen marked cell into two each; its new $2\times2$ block has three
markings, with the chosen type twice, the other type once, and one empty
corner, and every new row and column again has one marking of each type.
Destabilization is the inverse operation.

Suppose a finite planar grid has four consecutive columns, labeled in order
$P,L,Q,R$, and two consecutive rows $H<K$. Its markings on those rows are
exactly
$$H:\ (P,b),(Q,\bar b),\qquad K:\ (L,a),(R,\bar a),$$
where $a,b\in\{O,X\}$ and a bar denotes the other type. The other marking
of column $P$ is in a row $T>K$; the other markings of columns $L,Q,R$
are in rows strictly below $H$. These hypotheses describe an overpassing
cap with columns $L,R$ and an underpassing segment from $P$ to $Q$,
crossing its left leg. Rows outside this specified pattern and columns
outside this consecutive block are arbitrary.

Insert a row $J$ immediately below $H$ and a column $U$ immediately to the
right of $Q$. There is the following certificate, where a column or row
label follows its markings under a commutation:

| Stage | Column order in the active block | Active row order | Operation from the preceding stage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | $P,L,Q,R$ | $H<K$ | Initial pattern |
| 1 | $P,L,Q,U,R$ | $J<H<K$ | Stabilize at $(Q,H)$ |
| 2 | $P,L,Q,R,U$ | $J<H<K$ | Commute $U,R$ |
| 3 | $P,L,Q,R,U$ | $J<K<H$ | Commute $H,K$ |
| 4 | $L,Q,R,P,U$ | $J<K<H$ | Commute $P$ successively past $L,Q,R$ |
| 5 | $L,Q,R,P,U$ | $J<H<K$ | Commute $H,K$ |
| 6 | $L,Q,R,P$ | $J<K$ | Destabilize, deleting $H,U$ |

$$H:\ (P,b),(U,\bar b),\quad J:\ (Q,\bar b),(U,b),\quad K:\ (L,a),(R,\bar a).$$
At stage 6 they are
$$J:\ (Q,\bar b),(P,b),\qquad K:\ (L,a),(R,\bar a).$$
All other markings are transported by the stated row or column operations.
Thus the final underpassing segment crosses the right leg of the cap.
The six displayed arrows are $S,C,C,C,C,S^{-1}$, with the fourth arrow
comprising three elementary commutations. All four choices of $(a,b)$ are
valid whenever the initial markings extend to the given oriented grid.
Applying horizontal or vertical reflection to the entire certificate gives
the corresponding opposite-side or minimum pattern, with vertical segments
still over.

This is a conditional finite grid certificate for the specified over-arch
patterns. It does not assert that every bridge approximation has these

is underpassing has been treated.

Suppose a finite grid has four consecutive columns $L,B,M,R$ and two
consecutive rows $H<K$. For $a\in\{O,X\}$, with $\bar a$ the opposite type,
its markings on those rows are exactly
$$H:\ (L,a),(M,\bar a),\qquad K:\ (M,a),(R,\bar a).$$
The other markings of $L,R$ lie below $H$. Column $B$ has its markings in
rows $D<H$ and $T>K$, in either orientation. Thus the capped strand runs
through the two horizontal segments $L$ to $M$ and $M$ to $R$, and is
underpassing at its crossing with $B$.

Four allowed grid moves produce a grid whose active column order is
$L,M,B,R$ and whose active rows have markings
$$H:\ (M,a),(R,\bar a),\qquad K:\ (L,a),(M,\bar a).$$
Its other markings are exactly those obtained by first exchanging columns
$B,M$ and then exchanging the contents of rows $H,K$. The latter
shared-endpoint row exchange is realized by a stabilization, one allowed
commutation, and a destabilization, rather than used as a primitive move.

More explicitly, first commute $B,M$. Insert a column $V$ immediately
right of $L$, between $L,M$, and a row $J$ between $H,K$, by stabilizing
at $(L,H)$. Then commute $J,K$ and destabilize the block in columns
$V,M$ and rows $H,K$. Delete the old column $M$ and old row $K$,
and rename $V$ as $M$ and $J$ as $K$. The complete certificate is:

| Stage | Active column order | Active row order | Marked rows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | $L,B,M,R$ | $H<K$ | $H:(L,a),(M,\bar a)$; $K:(M,a),(R,\bar a)$ |
| 1 | $L,M,B,R$ | $H<K$ | Same labeled markings |
| 2 | $L,V,M,B,R$ | $H<J<K$ | $H:(V,a),(M,\bar a)$; $J:(L,a),(V,\bar a)$; $K:(M,a),(R,\bar a)$ |
| 3 | $L,V,M,B,R$ | $H<K<J$ | Same labeled markings as stage 2 |

Initially $B$ crosses the lower segment on the left side of the capped

derivations.claim: Take an ordinary bridge rectification of the first side using [F1]. Initially its designated columns need not be consecutive. For an overpassing maximum, write its cap row as $K$ with legs $L<R$, and its nearby crossing row as $H<K$. The crossing-containing underpassing join has one endpoint outside the cap and one inside. Its upper incident piece must be outside: an inside upper piece would continue above $K$, since no special height intervenes, and would cross the allegedly empty cap. By horizontal reflection of the coordinate recipe and, if necessary, reversing the move, the column order is $P<L<Q<R$, with $P$ the upper incident piece and $Q$ the lower one. Thus its row and partner data are those of [F3], except for column consecutiveness. For an underpassing maximum, the overpassing branch continues through the whole band as one vertical piece $B$, while the underpassing branch has a short piece $M$ between its crossing row $H$ and cap row $K$. The same empty-cap test puts these columns in order $L<B<M<R$, up to the same choices of side and move direction. These are exactly the non-adjacency parts of [F4]. The two rows are consecutive because no other special height intervenes. [F1, given, construct, cases]

Every other original column strictly between the leftmost and rightmost of the four designated columns has its entire closed vertical interval below $H$ or above $K$. In the overpassing case a column present at height $K$ between $L,R$ would cross the empty cap. A column between $P,L$ present at $H$ would add a second crossing to row $H$. The same argument covers the remaining subintervals, using the empty cap or the fact that the crossing row contains exactly its designated crossing. Since no old marking row is strictly between $H,K$, a foreign interval cannot meet just one interior part of the band without containing $H$ or $K$. Its endpoints cannot equal $H,K$, whose marks are already the four designated endpoints. For the underpassing case, the cap $[M,R]$ and the one-crossing join $[L,M]$ give the identical exclusion. Thus all foreign intervals in the relevant column span miss the entire closed band. [step 1.1, given, construct, cases]

Let $H_-$ be the old row immediately below $H$ and $K_+$ the old row immediately above $K$; if either is absent use an arbitrary exterior level on that side. Each lower incident designated piece has its other endpoint in a row at or below $H_-$. In the overpassing case these lower pieces are $L,Q,R$, in that left-to-right order. Split them by [F2], inserting a new lower anchor column immediately right of each original column and moving its crossing-free jog row to heights $$H_-<j_L<j_Q<j_R<H.$$ The original columns now contain only the upper pieces beginning at these cut rows; the new lower anchor for $C$ has interval ending at $j_C$. In the underpassing case do the same for $L,B,R$ with $$H_-<j_L<j_B<j_R<H.$$ The short column $M$ is not cut. All new row levels lie in the formerly empty gap, and all mark types are exactly those prescribed in [F2], with the original lower-end type used separately on each piece. The sweeps remain legal even past an earlier inserted cut row, since the two columns of the newly inserted jog are adjacent and the earlier row has neither endpoint on them. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

Cut the unique upper incident piece as well: it is $P$ in the first case and $B$ in the second. If its upper mark has type $d$ in row $T$, insert an anchor immediately right of its column and a row $i$ immediately below $T$, replace the old mark by $d$ in the original column at $i$, $\bar d$ in the anchor at $i$, and $d$ in the anchor at $T$. With north row $T$ and south row $i$, northwest is empty, northeast and southwest have $d$, and southeast has $\bar d$, so this is an allowed stabilization. Sweep the short row downward to $$K<i<K_+$$ by the same disjoint-or-strictly-nested test as in [F2]. The original upper piece is now bounded above by $i$, while its upper anchor starts at $i$. For $B$ this is done after its lower cut, so its localized interval is $[j_B,i]$. Each old foreign interval in step 2.1 is either below every lower cut or above $i$, since its endpoints are old row levels. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct]

Bring the four localized original columns together, preserving their order, by moving each of them left past intervening inactive columns, one adjacent exchange at a time. Every such exchange has disjoint closed intervals. Foreign old columns are disjoint from every localized piece by the preceding three cut and exclusion constructions. The upper anchor, if before a later localized column, starts above $K$, while that later column ends at or below $K$. A lower anchor for a designated piece can occur before a later lower localized piece only in the same left-to-right order used for the cut heights; its interval ends at an earlier $j$, strictly below that later piece's lower cut. In the underpassing case it may also precede the short $M$, whose interval starts at $H$ and is therefore disjoint from every lower anchor. No exchange of inactive columns with each other is needed: this is the finite stable sorting which puts the four distinguished letters before all intervening inactive letters while retaining the order within each list. Every inversion just enumerated is disjoint. The four localized columns are now consecutive and in the original designated order. The rows $H,K$ remain consecutive. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, construct, cases]

Apply [F3] or [F4] to this actual grid. Its hypotheses now hold literally. Lower partner heights are the cut rows below $H$, the unique upper partner is $i>K$, and the short $M$ has its original two endpoint rows. The certificates give genuine finite grid moves, not switches as extra primitives. In the overpassing case the four surviving localized columns end in order $L,Q,R,P$. The relative order of the lower incident pieces $L,Q,R$ is unchanged. In the underpassing case they end in order $L,M,B,R$, and the relative order of the lower incident pieces $L,B,R$ is unchanged. The unique upper incident piece is the same in either case. Rename the surviving crossing and cap levels $H,K$: the certificate inserts levels only immediately beside the interacting levels, so the new crossing remains above every lower cut and the cap below the upper cut. Every original marking outside the localized columns and interacting rows is transported exactly as asserted by those certificates. [F3, F4, step 4.1, construct, cases]

Check the cut rows after the certificate, since they cannot be dismissed as harmless without proof. At a lower cut row $j_C$, the jog joins its localized column to its lower anchor, which remains in the inactive list to the right of all four localized columns. A later lower localized piece starts at a strictly larger cut height and is absent at $j_C$; an earlier lower localized piece is to the left of $C$, in both the initial and final orders. A lower anchor with an earlier cut ends below $j_C$, and an anchor with a later cut lies after $C$'s anchor in the retained inactive order. The short $M$, when present, starts at $H>j_C$, and the upper-only piece $P$, when present, also starts at $H$. Upper anchors and old foreign columns are absent at all these cut heights. Thus no vertical segment lies in the interior of the cut row's horizontal interval. At the upper cut $i$, all other localized pieces end at or below $K$, all lower anchors end below $H$, and every old foreign upper interval begins at or above $K_+>i$; that jog is empty too. Each cut jog is monotone, because its two incident legs run respectively into the lower and upper parts of the same original oriented strand. All these statements remain true after the local column permutations, because the lower-piece order was retained in step 5.1. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, cases]

Every old horizontal row outside $H,K$ lies outside the localized vertical range, except for the newly inserted cut rows just checked. Its markings and crossing order therefore cannot acquire an extra crossing from the local certificates. Its old upper or lower continuation is carried by the same inactive anchor as before. The two interacting rows have exactly the cap and crossing patterns on the other side of the slide, by [F3] or [F4]. Consequently the output is a generalized bridge rectification: it has the original exterior bridge data, the desired new local bridge data, and only the empty monotone jogs of step 6.1. Its oriented strand incidence and crossing decorations agree with the desired second diagram. The ordered-graph bridge-isotopy construction in [F1] identifies these data; for regular jogs its exact extension is included in [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

Remove all regular jogs using [F2]. It supplies an actual finite move sequence to an ordinary bridge-like grid of the second bridge-isotopy class. Finally [F1] connects that grid to any prescribed rectification of the second side, and likewise permits any initial rectification. Horizontal reflection of the finite coordinate recipes handles the opposite side, vertical reflection handles a minimum in place of a maximum, and reversal handles either time direction; these recipes preserve vertical-over data. The independent marking choices in [F3] and [F4] cover both orientations of both strands. We have used only proved local certificates, reversible marked jog refinements and disjoint commutations, so no planar-invariance or global-generation premise has entered the argument. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 7.1, construct, cases] ∎

Consequently, if two nonempty oriented bridge diagrams differ by a single ordinary local birth/death of height-critical points, their bridge rectifications are related by grid moves. This conclusion uses no grid-isotopy generation theorem or crossing-slide realization.

At that time two spatially distinct special points have equal height and exchange height order transversely. Each is a nondegenerate height maximum, a nondegenerate height minimum, or a transverse crossing with neither branch height-critical. All other special heights are distinct and different from this common height, no other bridge degeneracy occurs, and the diagrams on either side are nonempty bridge diagrams. Then there are bridge-like grid rectifications on the two sides with identical column order and all but two row orders identical. The remaining adjacent rows have disjoint closed marking intervals and exchange by one legal row commutation, meaning the exchange of two adjacent rows whose closed horizontal marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. The oriented markings and crossing decorations are transported unchanged. All other choices of rectification on either side are connected to these by commutations.

Assume countable choice. Let two nonempty oriented bridge diagrams differ by one crossing sliding through one nondegenerate height extremum of a branch. The other branch is not height-critical, the crossing decorations are unchanged, and no other special height lies between these two interacting special heights on either sufficiently close side. Then any ordinary bridge-like grid rectifications of the two sides are connected by finitely many marked stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations, with the row $O$-to-$X$, column $X$-to-$O$, and vertical-over conventions. The height-critical branch may be overpassing or underpassing, and every orientation and maximum/minimum variant is included. No condition is imposed on the exterior strands or their remote endpoint heights.

A legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. The stabilizations and destabilizations are the usual three-mark two-by-two split and its inverse. In particular a shared-endpoint switch is not taken as a primitive grid move. No global grid-isotopy generation assertion is used.

derivations.claim: Reparameterize the given planar isotopy to be stationary on small endpoint collars: compose time with a smooth nondecreasing function that is zero near $0$, one near $1$, and strictly increasing between those collars. This changes neither endpoint diagram nor decorated planar class. Apply [F1] relative to those collars. Its finite exceptional times can be ordered $t_1<\cdots<t_N$. Around each choose a closed interval $[a_i,b_i]$ containing that time in its interior, with bridge endpoints, no other exceptional time, and pairwise disjoint intervals in their original order. If $N=0$, there are no such intervals. The complement consists of finitely many intervals all of whose diagrams are bridge diagrams. [F1, given, construct]

On a complementary interval there are no critical births, no crossing-critical coincidence and no special-height equality. Its critical points and crossing preimages continue smoothly, with unchanged orientation, decorations and strict order of special heights. Thus this restricted family is a bridge isotopy. By [F2] any rectifications of its two endpoints are connected by a finite sequence of legal column commutations. This includes constant complementary intervals and intervals containing no crossings: the asserted uniqueness concerns the full finite piece order, not a nonzero crossing count. At $t_i$ exactly one of the three kinds in [F1] occurs. Shrink $[a_i,b_i]$ if necessary. A birth/death has an isolated immersed local model and no crossing there, so [F3] applies. A coincidence of two spatially distinct special points has precisely the hypotheses of [F4]. These three cases exhaust [F1]. Each supplier connects arbitrary rectifications at the two endpoints, retaining all exterior strands, orientations and crossing decorations. No compatibility choice between neighboring local certificates is therefore required. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, cases]

Choose a rectification at each of the finitely many subdivision endpoints by [F2], keeping the two prescribed grids at $0,1$. Use step 2.1 on every complementary interval and step 2.2 on every exceptional interval. Their terminal and initial grids agree at the chosen shared endpoints, so concatenation is an actual finite sequence of the stated grid moves from the first prescribed grid to the second. When $N=0$ only step 2.1 is needed. Reversing any constituent sequence is permitted because commutations and the stabilization/destabilization pair are reversible. Consequently all choices of bridge representatives and rectifications in the same planar class give one grid-move class. Only the finite-event and proved local suppliers have been used. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct] ∎

Use oriented marked grids with vertical segments over horizontal ones. A stabilization splits one row and column through a chosen marking into a three-mark two-by-two block: the chosen type occurs twice at opposite corners, the other type once, and the last corner is empty; one mark of each type remains in every row and column. A commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed marking intervals. In the patterns below $\bar a$ denotes the other type from $a\in\{O,X\}$, and all unspecified markings belong to an arbitrary valid exterior grid.

The following are marked grid certificates for R1, R2 and R3, respectively.

* R1: choose a corner $(P,H)$ of type $a$, its row partner $(B,H)$ of type $\bar a$ with $P<B$, and its column partner $(P,T)$ with $H<T$. Insert $C$ immediately left of $P$ and $H'$ immediately above $H$. Replace the old row marks by $(P,H,a),(C,H,\bar a),(C,H',a),(B,H',\bar a)$. This one stabilization inserts one Reidemeister kink, up to planar isotopy.
* R2: suppose $P,R$ are adjacent columns in that order, $K<H$ are consecutive rows, and the closed vertical interval of $P$ has endpoints $V<K<H<T$. Column $R$ has endpoints $K,H$. The row marks are $H:(A,a),(R,\bar a)$ and $K:(D,\bar a),(R,a)$, where $A,D<P$, the other endpoint of $A$ is above $H$, and that of $D$ is below $K$. Commuting $P,R$ removes the two crossings of $P$ with these rows and realizes R2.
* R3: suppose $P,R$ are adjacent columns in that order and $K<L<H$ are three consecutive rows. Column $P$ has endpoints $V<K<H<T$, and column $R$ has endpoints $K,H$. The row marks are $H:(A,a),(R,\bar a)$, $K:(R,a),(C,\bar a)$ and $L:(D,b),(E,\bar b)$, with $D<A<P<R<C<E$. The other endpoint of $A$ is above $H$, and that of $C$ is below $K$. Commuting $P,R$ realizes R3: the crossing between the top strand $P$ and the middle strand moves from row $H$ to row $K$, while the two crossings with the bottom strand in row $L$ change order.

In R2 and R3 the two types on column $P$ may be chosen in either order, subject to being part of the given grid. All indicated orientation choices, both directions of each move, and the horizontally and vertically reflected coordinate recipes are allowed. These models include every local sign/orientation variant of R1 and R2 and every consistent strict over/under height order and orientation variant of R3. The assertion is about these explicit finite models; a relative rectangularization placing an arbitrary surrounding diagram into their adjacency patterns is a separate obligation.

Assume countable choice. In a nonempty generic marked rectangular diagram call a horizontal segment a cap if its two incident vertical segments extend to the same side in height, and monotone otherwise. A generalized bridge rectification has three kinds of horizontal segment: an empty cap, a monotone segment with exactly one crossing, and an empty monotone segment, called a regular jog. Smooth the first two kinds as in a bridge-like grid and tilt and round each regular jog monotonically in height. This produces a bridge diagram with one distinguished regular point for each jog, at pairwise distinct heights different from all critical and crossing heights. For a jog remember also whether its lower incident vertical piece is to the left or to the right of its upper incident piece. This is its side datum.

Two generalized bridge rectifications whose smoothed diagrams with distinguished points are bridge isotopic, with the same side data, are connected by finitely many disjoint-interval column commutations after normalization of coordinate orders. Every generalized bridge rectification is related by finite grid stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations to an ordinary bridge-like grid whose smoothing has the same bridge-isotopy class after forgetting the distinguished regular points.

More explicitly, a vertical grid piece in column $P$ from a mark $a$ at lower row $L$ to its complementary mark at upper row $T$ may be split at any regular height $L<h<T$. Insert $Q$ immediately right of $P$ and $J$ immediately above $L$, replace $(P,L,a)$ by $(P,J,a),(Q,J,\bar a),(Q,L,a)$, and commute the short row $J$ to the gap containing $h$. Here $\bar a$ is the other marking type. This inserts a crossing-free jog with the lower piece on the right. Insertion to the left gives the other side. These constructions, their inverses, and the preceding uniqueness assertion do not use global grid-isotopy generation.

A legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. A stabilization replaces a marking by a three-mark two-by-two block with its type twice at opposite corners, the complementary type once, and one empty corner, preserving one of each type per row and column.

Let $G$ be a finite nonempty planar marked grid with vertical-over crossing convention. A horizontal segment is a cap if its two incident vertical segments both extend above it or both extend below it; otherwise it is monotone. A marked stabilization splits a marked cell into a two-by-two block with the chosen marking type twice at opposite corners, the other type once and one empty corner, preserving one of each type per row and column. A legal column commutation exchanges adjacent columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed vertical marking intervals. There is a finite sequence of marked stabilizations and legal commutations carrying $G$ to a grid in which every cap has no crossing and every monotone horizontal segment has exactly one crossing. Thus the resulting grid is bridge-like: slightly tilt its crossing-containing horizontal segments in the direction of height travel and round its empty caps to obtain a bridge diagram. Every operation respects the oriented $O,X$ convention of the grid-diagram definition, and the number of link components is unchanged. The decorated planar diagram before and after the entire refinement is planar isotopic after rounding corners; in particular no Reidemeister move is needed for this refinement. No global grid-move generation theorem is assumed.

Assume countable choice. Let $D_0,D_1$ be nonempty oriented bridge diagrams that are planar isotopic with crossing decorations transported by the isotopy. Then any bridge-like grid rectification of $D_0$ is connected to any bridge-like grid rectification of $D_1$ by finitely many marked grid stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations. Here vertical strands pass over horizontal strands, a legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns with disjoint or strictly nested closed marking intervals, and a stabilization is a three-mark two-by-two split preserving one $O$ and one $X$ per row and column. In particular the grid-move class assigned by bridge rectification depends only on the oriented decorated planar-isotopy class whenever that class is represented by bridge diagrams. No Reidemeister-move or global grid-isotopy generation theorem is used.

derivations.claim: First choose the finite local rectangular tangle of [F1] for the specified move. Its strands and boundary cyclic order are those of the given Reidemeister disk: the R1 model is one immersed arc with one kink, R2 has a single excursion across the other arc and back, and R3 has the top, middle and bottom arcs with the same three pairwise boundary incidences. The variants in [F1] include their reverse boundary cyclic orders and all oriented decorations. Extend the local tangle slightly along its boundary arcs so that its ends are vertical and its horizontal joins lie strictly inside a rectangle $B=[c,d]\times[a,b]$; the vertical ends meet only the top or bottom of $B$. This can be done in disjoint boundary collars: continue each rectangular leg until its first horizontal turn is inside $B$, and put its next vertical end at the boundary. Preserve the cyclic order of these ends. An order-preserving matching of finitely many boundary ports extends to a smooth increasing angular map of their boundary circles: interpolate with positive derivative in the gaps, then interpolate its angular lift with the identity. Applying that map in a boundary collar matches the old and new attachment ports. The chosen local model and the given local diagram are planar equivalent as decorated arcs relative to their boundary incidence: straighten their finitely many embedded edge strips, match their small crossing disks using the same branch order, and interpolate monotonically across the intervening empty strips. Thus one may attach the original exterior to this rectangular tangle without changing the planar class on either side of the move. Only the local tangle, and not the exterior, is replaced at this stage. [F1, given, construct, cases]

We give the relative rectangular extension used for that attachment. A finite smooth decorated diagram outside the fixed tangle can be made rectangular without adding crossings, while keeping the tangle and its short vertical boundary collars fixed. Choose disjoint small disks at its finitely many exterior crossings, and in each use the two transverse branches as local coordinates. Replace their smaller cores by a horizontal underpassing segment and a vertical overpassing segment, attaching in the annular collars in the same four-sector order. This is a plane isotopy of the decorated crossing: the local coordinate diffeomorphism matches the two crossing arcs, and the four remaining disjoint edge strips extend the matching by increasing interval coordinates. The remaining finitely many embedded arcs have disjoint thin neighborhoods, except for their prescribed end collars. Subdivide each arc into finitely many patches in which one Cartesian coordinate is strictly monotone. Inside such a patch approximate its graph by a finite orthogonal staircase with the same end collars: choose a sufficiently fine partition in the monotone coordinate, put each horizontal or vertical step inside the corresponding small graph rectangle, and connect consecutive steps there. Rectangles of nonadjacent subarcs can be chosen disjoint by compact separation. At a common end use a smaller empty patch to connect the two paths, removing immediate backtracking. Round the staircase slightly to be a graph in that patch. Linear interpolation of its graph function with the old graph, in a smaller graph strip, is an isotopy; increasing transverse-coordinate maps extend it to the strip and are the identity at its boundary. These finitely many strip isotopies establish the asserted planar equivalence, not merely a close approximation. No path enters $B$ except its prescribed end collar. [given, construct]

Choose all newly introduced horizontal levels and vertical columns distinct from each other and from the finitely many fixed model levels and columns, except when they are portions of the same straight piece. The staircase construction permits this: make each new turn inside an open empty patch, choose its coordinate avoiding a finite set, and keep successive coordinates within that patch; combine consecutive collinear pieces first. The fixed vertical end collars extend only until their first exterior turn, so each continues its one fixed model column, rather than creating another segment in that column. No two such fixed continuations have the same column. Likewise each fixed model horizontal join remains its sole segment at its level. Consequently every horizontal segment has its own row and every vertical segment its own column. Orient the resulting closed orthogonal curves. At each corner put $O$ when the outgoing edge is horizontal and $X$ when it is vertical. Along every horizontal edge the initial mark is $O$ and terminal mark $X$, and along every vertical edge they are $X,O$; this is independent of the directions left/right or up/down. Thus there is one mark of each type in every row and column. The model's marks agree with these because its oriented certificate uses exactly the same convention. The result is an actual grid $G$ extending the chosen local tangle, with its original exterior planar diagram, not just an unmarked rectangular picture. [F1, step 1.2, construct]

We now make the required model rows and columns consecutive by actual moves. All model horizontal joins lie in the interior of $B$ and all model vertical pieces meeting its height band are the designated pieces. A foreign vertical column between the extreme model columns therefore has interval entirely below $a$ or entirely above $b$: its connected vertical segment lies outside $B$. Cut each designated piece that exits below $B$ at a distinct height in the empty gap immediately below $a$, choosing the cuts strictly increasing in left-to-right column order. Insert its lower anchor immediately to its right by [F2]; the original column retains only the upper localized piece. Cut each piece exiting above $B$ in the gap immediately above $b$, with cut heights strictly decreasing in left-to-right order. Use the reflected upper-end version of [F2], retaining the lower localized piece and putting its upper anchor immediately to its right. Explicitly, at an upper endpoint $(P,T,d)$ introduce $i<T$ and its right neighbor $Q$, remove that mark and put $(P,i,d),(Q,i,\bar d),(Q,T,d)$; the empty northwest block is a legal stabilization, and the short row sweeps down by the adjacent-column disjoint-or-nested test of [F2]. All cuts can be chosen nearer to $[a,b]$ than every foreign old endpoint level, since there are finitely many. [F2, step 2.1, construct]

Stable-sort the localized model columns together to the left of the intervening inactive columns, retaining the orders in each list. Every inversion is disjoint. A foreign old column ends below every lower cut or starts above every upper cut. A lower anchor for an earlier model column ends below the lower endpoint of any later model column that exits downward, by increasing lower cuts; a later model column that does not exit downward starts inside $[a,b]$ instead. An earlier upper anchor starts above the endpoint of any later model column that exits upward, by decreasing upper cuts; a later column not exiting upward ends inside the band. Hence each adjacent exchange is a legal disjoint-column commutation. The localized columns now have exactly their model adjacency. A foreign row inside $[a,b]$ has its whole horizontal segment to the left or to the right of $B$, because the extended exterior avoids $B$; its interval is therefore disjoint from every model horizontal join. Clear such foreign rows from between the model levels by adjacent row commutations, retaining their relative order. The localized column sorting has kept the model columns inside their original extreme column span and has changed no endpoint of these foreign rows; those disjointness tests remain valid. The model rows required in [F1] are now consecutive. The added cut rows are outside their band. The fitted input still has the old decorated planar class: cutting introduces a monotone empty jog, and the disjoint column and row sweeps move only disjoint height pieces or disjoint horizontal joins. Their crossing lists and cyclic vertex orders are unchanged; increasing graph-coordinate maps on the empty strips, as constructed in step 1.2, give plane isotopies. [step 3.1, construct, cases]

Apply the exact finite certificate of [F1]. All its hypotheses hold literally in this grid. The cut rows supply the exterior endpoints of the long local columns where required; short internal columns and their endpoint rows are unchanged. The certificate fixes all exterior marked incidence and preserves the boundary order of both the upper and lower emerging pieces, since it is the stated Reidemeister tangle relative to its boundary. The cut joins remain empty monotone jogs: at a lower cut, earlier lower localized pieces lie to its left, later ones start higher, earlier lower anchors have already ended and later anchors lie beyond its anchor. Upper anchors are absent there. At an upper cut the reversed height ordering gives the same check: earlier upper localized pieces lie to its left, later ones end lower, earlier upper anchors have not started and later anchors lie beyond its anchor. Lower anchors are absent there. Foreign old columns miss all these cut heights. These assertions hold before and after the local certificate because the boundary orders are retained. Thus smoothing the output gives exactly the second Reidemeister diagram with the same exterior, plus these monotone jogs; no extra crossing is introduced by fitting or by the certificate. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, cases]

Refine both the fitted input and its output using [F3]. Their smoothings are planar isotopic to the originally prescribed two endpoint diagrams by the relative construction just proved and the planar-isotopy clause of [F3]. The refinements themselves are grid moves. The arbitrary prescribed bridge rectifications connect to these two refined grids by [F4]. Concatenate the reverse first refinement, the fitted local certificate, the second refinement, and the endpoint identifications. This gives a finite sequence from any prescribed initial rectification to any prescribed final rectification. The model choice in [F1] covers every allowed sign and orientation, and all fitting arguments depended only on ordered empty collars and finite exterior separation. This proves the full assertion with arbitrary exterior data. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

On this page the scalar field is the field $\mathbb R$ of real numbers: $X$, $Y$
and $Z$ always denote real Banach spaces ([[def-banach-space]]) and $U
\subseteq X$ always denotes an open subset of $X$, in the metric topology of the
norm ([[def-metric-topology]]).

Let $f : U \to Y$ be a map and let $x \in U$. For a bounded linear operator
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) write

$$r(h) := f(x+h) - f(x) - Th \qquad (h \in X,\ x+h \in U).$$

Then $f$ is **Fréchet differentiable at $x$** when there is
$T \in \mathcal B(X,Y)$ with

$$\lim_{\substack{h \to 0 \\ h \ne 0}} \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-Th\|}{\|h\|} = 0 ,$$

the limit being taken over those $h$ with $x + h \in U$. Such an operator $T$ is
a **Fréchet derivative of $f$ at $x$**, written $T = Df(x)$, and $\|T\|$ is its
operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). When $f$ is Fréchet differentiable at
every point of $U$, $f$ is **differentiable on $U$** and the **derivative** is
the map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$, $x \mapsto Df(x)$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be real Banach spaces and let $U \subseteq X$ be open. All
derivatives below are Fréchet derivatives
([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]), and all continuity is with
respect to the norm metrics ([[def-metric-continuity]]).

* $f : U \to Y$ is of **class $C^0$** when $f$ is continuous on $U$.
* $f$ is of **class $C^1$** when $f$ is differentiable on $U$ and its derivative
  map $Df : U \to \mathcal B(X,Y)$ is continuous for the operator norm on
  $\mathcal B(X,Y)$ ([[def-operator-norm]],
  [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]).
* For $k \ge 1$ define the spaces of iterated derivative values by
  $$\mathcal B_0 := Y, \qquad \mathcal B_{k} := \mathcal B(X,\mathcal B_{k-1}).$$
  Each $\mathcal B_k$ is a real Banach space for the operator norm, by induction
  on $k$ from [[thm-bounded-operator-space-is-banach]]. Then $f$ is of **class
  $C^{k}$** when $f$ is of class $C^{k-1}$, the map
  $D^{k-1}f : U \to \mathcal B_{k-1}$ is differentiable on $U$, where
  $D^0f := f$, and the **$k$-th derivative**
  $D^k f : U \to \mathcal B_k$ is continuous for the operator norm on
  $\mathcal B_k$. We write $D^kf(x)$ for the value at $x$.
* $f$ is of **class $C^\infty$** when $f$ is of class $C^k$ for every $k \ge 0$.

For open sets $U \subseteq X$ and $V \subseteq Y$, a map $f : U \to V$ is a
**$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when it is a bijection, $f$ is of class $C^k$ and
$f^{-1} : V \to U$ is of class $C^k$; likewise with $C^\infty$ in place of
$C^k$.

derivations.claim: We first establish the needed mean-value estimate without selecting a dual functional. If a differentiable Banach-valued path $g$ on $[a,b]$ has $\|g'(t)\|\le C$, then $\phi(t)=\|g(t)-g(a)\|$ has upper right Dini derivative at most $C$, by the derivative remainder and the triangle inequality. For $\eta>0$, put $h(t)=\phi(t)-(C+\eta)(t-a)$. If $h(b)>h(a)$, its minimum on the compact interval is attained at some $t_0<b$; all sufficiently small right differences there are nonnegative, contradicting the strictly negative upper right Dini derivative. Thus $\phi(b)\le(C+\eta)(b-a)$; let $\eta\downarrow0$. Applying this argument to each subinterval proves the segment estimate $\|g(b)-g(a)\|\le C(b-a)$. For a continuous Banach-valued function, its dyadic Riemann sums are Cauchy by uniform continuity, hence converge by completeness; comparison with arbitrary fine partitions identifies the same integral. The difference-quotient estimate for this integral gives its derivative equal to the integrand. The segment estimate just proved makes a differentiable path with zero derivative constant. Consequently the Banach-valued fundamental theorem holds for $C^1$ paths. Applied to $N(z)=f(z)-f(0)-Dz$, it gives $$\|N(z)\|\le\tfrac{L}{2}\|z\|^2,\qquad \|N(z)-N(w)\|\le Lr\|z-w\|$$ on the closed radius-$r$ ball. The first bound integrates $\|(df(tz)-D)z\|\le Lt\|z\|^2$; the second uses the segment estimate and $\|dN\|\le Lr$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

The operators $QD$ and $P=I_E-QD$ are bounded complementary projections: $(QD)^2=QD$, $DP=0$, $P|_{\ker D}=I$, and $QD$ is the identity on $V=\operatorname{im}Q$. Their ranges are closed, since a bounded projection's range is the kernel of its complementary projection. Thus $E=K\oplus V$, and the closed ball in $V$ is complete. On the radius-$\rho$ ball in $V$, $\rho=2M\varepsilon<r$, define $T(z)=-Qf(0)-QN(z)$. Step 1.1 and $MLr\le1/2$ give $$\|T(z)\|\le M\varepsilon+MLr\|z\|\le\rho,\qquad \|T(z)-T(w)\|\le\tfrac12\|z-w\|.$$ Starting with $x_0=0$, iterate this one prescribed map. Its increments are at most $2^{-n}\|x_1-x_0\|$, so the geometric tail bound makes the sequence Cauchy and complete convergence gives a fixed point $x$. If $\varepsilon=0$ the ball is the singleton zero and the same conclusion holds directly. On $V$, applying $D$ to $z=T(z)$ gives $Dz=-f(0)-N(z)$, hence $f(z)=0$; conversely every zero in $V$ satisfies this fixed-point identity because $QDz=z$. The Lipschitz estimate holds on the entire radius-$r$ ball, so any two zeros in that larger ball coincide as well. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

The norm bound is $\|x\|\le\rho$. The equation $x+Qf(0)=-QN(x)$ and the quadratic bound of step 1.1 give $$\|x+Qf(0)\|\le\tfrac{ML}{2}\rho^2=2M^3L\varepsilon^2.$$ Write $A=(df(x)-D)Q$. Then $\|A\|\le LM\|x\|\le MLr\le1/2$. The explicit series $\sum_{n\ge0}(-A)^n$ converges in bounded-operator norm, since its tails have geometric norm bounds and the operator space is complete pointwise with the uniform limit bound. Multiplication of finite partial sums and passage to the limit show that it is a two-sided inverse of $I_Y+A$, of norm at most two. Therefore $df(x)Q_x=(I_Y+A)(I_Y+A)^{-1}=I_Y$, and $\|Q_x\|\le2M$. No choice of a new complement or inverse has been made. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

We prove the local chart, including its parameter version, directly. Replace $D$ by $d_zf(p_0,0)$, use the fixed splitting of step 2.1, and set $$T(p,k,w)=w-Qf(p,k+w),\qquad w\in V.$$ Its derivative in $w$ is $I_V-Qd_zf(p,k+w)|_V$, which vanishes at $(p_0,0,0)$. Choose product neighborhoods with $\|d_wT\|\le1/2$ there, by continuity. Choose a closed $V$-ball of radius $b>0$ inside this product, then shrink the open parameter and $K$ neighborhoods so $\|T(p,k,0)\|<b/2$. The segment estimate in step 1.1 makes $T(p,k,\cdot)$ a contraction of that closed ball into itself. Its explicit iteration from zero gives a unique fixed point $v(p,k)$. Since $Q$ is injective ($DQ=I$), the fixed-point equation is equivalent to $f(p,k+v)=0$. Any zero in the product neighborhood is that fixed point. The fixed point is interior because its norm is at most $2\|T(p,k,0)\|<b$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

The fixed point depends continuously, and locally Lipschitz, on $(p,k)$. For two nearby parameters $a,a'$ denoting this combined variable, subtract the fixed-point equations to obtain $$\|v(a')-v(a)\|\le2\|T(a',v(a))-T(a,v(a))\|.$$ Continuity gives continuity; a bounded derivative in the parameter variable on a sufficiently small product ball gives local Lipschitz dependence by step 1.1. Put $H=I_V-d_wT(a,v(a))$. Its Neumann inverse has norm at most two. For a small parameter increment $h$, the $C^1$ remainder, and the Lipschitz bound on $v$, give $$H\bigl(v(a+h)-v(a)\bigr)=d_aT(a,v(a))h+o(\|h\|).$$ Thus $v$ is differentiable, with $$dv(a)=\bigl[I_V-d_wT(a,v(a))\bigr]^{-1}d_aT(a,v(a)).$$ All factors are continuous; hence $v$ is $C^1$. When there is no parameter $p$, at $k=0$ one has $v(0)=0$ and $d_kT=-QD|_K=0$, so $dv(0)=0$. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra]

For completeness, the derivative rules just used require no hidden selection principle. The chain rule follows by substituting the two norm-remainder expansions, with local boundedness of the first derivative controlling the inner remainder. The product rule follows by expanding a bounded bilinear product and bounding the product of the two increments. On the open set of invertible bounded operators, the identity $$ (A+H)^{-1}-A^{-1}=-(A+H)^{-1}HA^{-1}$$ and the Neumann norm bound show continuity; substituting it once more gives derivative $H\mapsto-A^{-1}HA^{-1}$ with quadratic remainder. Differentiating this finite product expression inductively proves smoothness of inversion. If $T$ is $C^q$, the derivative formula in step 4.1 is therefore $C^{j-1}$ whenever $v$ is $C^{j-1}$ and $j\le q$. Induction upgrades $v$ to $C^q$, including every finite order when $q=\infty$. These arguments also prove the smoothness of the explicit linear splitting coordinate maps and the resulting zero-set parametrization $k\mapsto k+v(k)$. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Finally suppose the right inverse varies smoothly with $p$. Work in the fixed space $Y$ and write the correction as $x=Q(p)y$. Put $D(p)=d_zf(p,0)$ and $N(p,z)=f(p,z)-f(p,0)-D(p)z$. The correction equation is exactly $$y=-f(p,0)-N(p,Q(p)y).$$ The right side also equals $y-f(p,Q(p)y)$, so it is $C^q$ without requiring an extra derivative of $D(p)$. At a fixed solution its derivative in $y$ has norm at most $LM\|x\|<1/2$. In a small product neighborhood of that fixed point and parameter, continuity gives a uniform contraction bound less than one. Shrink a closed ball about that fixed point and then the parameter neighborhood so the map preserves that ball, as in step 3.2. The local contraction and differentiability proof in the three preceding chart steps thus applies in $Y$ to give a $C^q$ family $y(p)$, hence $x(p)=Q(p)y(p)$. Uniqueness from step 2.1 identifies it with the quantitative correction. The zero target or zero kernel cases are included: the relevant ball is a singleton and the stated maps and formulas still apply. All infinite objects used were explicit convergent sequences or series, so no stronger choice axiom entered. This proves all assertions. [step 2.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, cases] ∎

Work in the smooth category inherited from the oriented-link convention. In particular, an embedded bridge witness disk means the image of a smooth rank-two embedding of a planar disk, with ordinary smooth boundary or smooth transverse corners at its two marked endpoints; smoothness at a boundary or corner means local smooth extension in its charts. Witness parametrizations can be chosen for the finite disk families. This category convention does not require the knot arcs to meet the Heegaard surface transversely: tangential smooth crossings remain permitted.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $h$, let $k\ge1$, and put $m=h+k-1$. A **handlebody** is a compact three-manifold that is a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph. A **$2k$-pointed Heegaard diagram for $S^3$** consists of a splitting $S^3=U_{\alpha}\cup_{\Sigma}U_{\beta}$ into handlebodies, two systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves on $\Sigma$ that bound pairwise disjoint properly embedded disks in $U_{\alpha}$ and $U_{\beta}$, respectively, cutting each handlebody into exactly $k$ three-balls, and two ordered sets of distinct points $\mathbf w=(w_1,\ldots,w_k)$ and $\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_k)$ disjoint from the curves. Curves from different systems intersect transversely in finitely many points. Each component of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$ contains exactly one $w$-point and exactly one $z$-point. The diagram also includes trivial arc systems in the two handlebodies: the $\alpha$-arcs join $w_i$ to $z_i$, and the $\beta$-arcs join $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$, with indices modulo $k$. Each system is disjoint from its compression disks and is simultaneously boundary parallel: its arcs cobound pairwise disjoint embedded disks with arcs in the corresponding components of the attaching-system complement on $\Sigma$. Thus each ball obtained by compression contains one unknotted arc. Together the arcs form an oriented knot, oriented from $w_i$ to $z_i$ in $U_{\alpha}$ and from $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$ in $U_{\beta}$. The diagram is **compatible with $K$** when this knot is orientation-preservingly ambient isotopic to $K$. For a grid diagram, compatibility uses the row and column orientation fixed in the grid definition, with $w$-points at $O$ and $z$-points at $X$. For a grid representing one knot, the basepoint pairs can be numbered cyclically in reverse order of travel along the oriented knot so that $w_i,z_i$ lie in the same component $A_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and $w_i,z_{i+1}$ lie in the same component $B_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$.

Comparisons of these embedded diagrams allow **orientation-preserving diagram isomorphisms**: an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ carrying the two handlebodies, their oriented Heegaard surface, the two attaching systems, the ordered $w,z$ points, and the two simultaneously boundary-parallel arc systems to the corresponding data. Equivalently one may specify the surface isomorphism together with its compatible collared extensions over both handlebodies carrying those arcs. The attaching systems are carried as systems; reordering their curve factors induces the corresponding product identification. Comparisons also allow **arc normalizations in the fixed splitting**: a smooth isotopy of the represented oriented knot, supported near the ordered marks and fixing each mark, during which every open connecting arc stays in its original handlebody and the two simultaneous boundary-parallel witness systems are retained or replaced by embedded witnesses for those same arcs. The surface, attaching curves, marked points and compression disks stay fixed. Such a normalization may replace a tangential marked crossing by a transverse one; the original data are not required to have neat arcs. This is a change of knot representative relative to the fixed surface, not a diagram isomorphism carrying both objects. Analytic and assigned grading data depending on the fixed surface diagram can be kept identical; the corresponding generator and disk-count identification is then the identity. Existence of normalizations with the required witnesses is a separate geometric assertion, not part of this definition. Such a comparison transports the represented oriented knot and any specified Seifert surface as well. For analytic data, it transports $j$, the surface area form, all chosen divisor neighborhoods and $J_t$ by the induced symmetric-product diffeomorphism. The comparison maps on generators and disk classes are their pushforwards under this map; compatibility with the count differential is a mathematical property to be proved. No identity action is part of this convention, even when the ambient diffeomorphism is isotopic to the identity.

The $m$-fold symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)=\Sigma^m/S_m$ is the space of unordered $m$-tuples of points of $\Sigma$, where $S_m$ permutes coordinates. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ be the quotient map. The product tori are the images $\mathbb T_{\alpha}=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_m)$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_m)$. Their intersection points are the generators. A **Whitney disk class** $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps from a disk to $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ whose two boundary arcs lie on $\mathbb T_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}$ and whose endpoints are $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions with coefficients equal to local multiplicities. Write $n_{w_i}(\phi)$ and $n_{z_i}(\phi)$ for its local multiplicities at the marked points. An almost complex structure $J$ on $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ is a smooth endomorphism of the tangent bundle with $J^2=-1$. Fix a complex structure $j$ and an area form on $\Sigma$. For $m>0$, choose a smooth path $\mathbb J=(J_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ of nearly symmetric almost complex structures, constant near $t=0,1$: each $J_t$ agrees with the induced integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(j)$ on a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and of every divisor $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ for a chosen interior point $p$ of every complementary region, including every marked point, and tames the form descended from the product area form off that neighborhood. The path is a sufficiently small perturbation in this class. For $m=0$ the symmetric product is a point. Local multiplicities are intersection numbers with these divisors; positivity is a mathematical property to be proved, not an additional choice of disk counts. A $\mathbb J$-holomorphic strip representative is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ satisfying $\partial_{\tau}u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with $u(\tau,0)\in\mathbb T_{\alpha}$, $u(\tau,1)\in\mathbb T_{\beta}$, and limits $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ as $\tau\to-\infty,+\infty$. Translation in $\tau$ defines an $\mathbb R$-action. The Maslov index $\mu(\phi)$ is the Fredholm index of the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at a representative of $\phi$; the relative Maslov grading convention is $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=\mu(\phi)-2\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_{w_i}(\phi)$, up to one overall additive constant.

A **periodic domain** is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of full $\alpha$- and $\beta$-curves; its local multiplicity at a marked point is the coefficient of the containing region. The pointed diagram is **admissible** when every nonzero periodic domain with $n_{w_i}=0$ for all $i$ has at least one positive and at least one negative region coefficient. A path $\mathbb J$ is **regular for a set of disk classes** when the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at every holomorphic-strip representative in those classes is surjective. For a path regular on the classes used, let $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)$ be the space of strip representatives. If, for each generator $\mathbf x$, only finitely many pairs $(\mathbf y,\phi)$ with $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing$, $\mu(\phi)=1$, and $n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0$ for every $i$ occur, and each quotient is finite, the multipointed full filtered minus module is the free module over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_k]$ generated by $\mathbb T_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb T_{\beta}$, with differential
$$\partial^-\mathbf x=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y),\;\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing\\\mu(\phi)=1,\; n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0\ \forall i}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)\,U_1^{n_{w_1}(\phi)}\cdots U_k^{n_{w_k}(\phi)}\mathbf y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is the count modulo two of the zero-dimensional quotient when it is finite. Quotienting by all $U_i$ leaves the fully blocked multipointed chain complex (the hat chain complex when $k=1$), with terms only from classes satisfying $n_{w_i}=0$ for every $i$; its Alexander-filtered associated-graded complex further retains only classes with every $n_{z_i}=0$. The relative Alexander grading convention is $A(\mathbf x)-A(\mathbf y)=\sum_i n_{z_i}(\phi)-\sum_i n_{w_i}(\phi)$, with an overall additive constant. Each $U_i$ lowers Maslov grading by two and Alexander filtration by one. In a grid diagram, $\Sigma=T^2$, $h=1$, $k=n$, and $m=n$; the horizontal circles are the $\alpha$-curves, the vertical circles are the $\beta$-curves, and the $w$-points and $z$-points are the $O$- and $X$-markings respectively.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

For $A\subseteq X$ there is an exact sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(A;G)\to H_n(X;G)\to H_n(X,A;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(A;G)\to H_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots.$$

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then for every $n\geq 0$ and
every abelian group $G$ the induced homomorphisms on singular homology agree:
$$H_n(f_\#)=H_n(g_\#):H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G)\to H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(Y;G).$$

Let
$$\cdots \to A_{n-1} \to A_n \to A_{n+1} \to A_{n+2} \to A_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
and
$$\cdots \to B_{n-1} \to B_n \to B_{n+1} \to B_{n+2} \to B_{n+3} \to \cdots$$
be long exact sequences in an abelian category, together with a morphism of
these sequences. If the four comparison maps at $A_{n-1},A_n,A_{n+2},A_{n+3}$
are isomorphisms, then the comparison map $A_{n+1} \to B_{n+1}$ is an
isomorphism.

Let $M$ be a compact $R$-oriented $n$-manifold with boundary $A$, where $R$ is commutative unital and orientation means the supplied orientation on $N=M\setminus A$. There is a unique class
$$z\in H_n(M,A;R)$$
whose restriction at every point of $N$ is the prescribed local generator. The connecting map sends $z$ to a class $\partial z\in H_{n-1}(A;R)$ whose restrictions are local generators at every boundary point. These restrictions form the induced orientation of $A$, and $\partial z$ is its fundamental class.

The sign convention is outward-normal-first. More explicitly, in coordinates consisting of $n-1$ tangent directions followed by an inward collar coordinate, the induced boundary generator is $(-1)^n$ times the tangent generator for the corresponding product orientation. Empty boundary and dimension zero are included. No AC is used.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

derivations.claim: Give the Heegaard surface a thin product collar in the splitting. In this smooth finite setting use the standard metric on $S^3$ and its oriented unit normal $N$ to the surface, with in the standard $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$, the explicit normal map $(p,t)\mapsto(p+tN(p))/\sqrt{1+t^2}$. Its derivative at zero is the tangent-plus-normal isomorphism. The inverse function theorem [F5] gives local product neighborhoods, while compact separation and a finite subcover give a common positive width and injectivity. Enlarge the interiors of both handlebodies through half this collar to an open cover of $S^3$. The two members retract to the respective handlebodies and their intersection retracts to $\Sigma$. By [F2] and homotopy invariance in [F3], the homomorphism $$H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H_1(U_\alpha;\mathbb Z)\oplus H_1(U_\beta;\mathbb Z)$$ induced by their inclusions is injective, since its preceding Mayer–Vietoris term is $H_2(S^3;\mathbb Z)=0$. Hence the kernels of the two individual inclusion maps have zero intersection. No intersection-pairing or full-choice surface duality theorem is needed. [F1, F2, F3, F5, given, construct, algebra]

We record the relative-domain calculation for any finite disjoint union $C$ of attaching circles on an oriented closed surface. A union of disjoint thin annuli about $C$ retracts to $C$; the annuli are supplied by a finite normal-coordinate construction: choose the oriented unit normal to each circle within the surface, move in that direction in $S^3$, and project back to $\Sigma$ using the first coordinate of its collar inverse from step1.1. At zero the two derivatives span the surface tangent plane; [F5] and compact separation give disjoint annuli of uniform positive width. Relative excision and these collar retractions in [F3] identify $$H_2(\Sigma,C;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_D H_2(\overline D,\partial\overline D;\mathbb Z),$$ where $D$ runs over the components of the surface cut along those annuli. There are finitely many such components: each additional circle increases the component count by at most one, since cutting a connected surface along one circle gives at most two components. Each summand is infinite cyclic on its oriented relative class. To verify this last assertion directly from [F4], restrict any relative class to an interior point, where its value is an integer times the positive local generator. The integer is locally constant: two nearby points lie inside one closed coordinate disk. Restrict first to its relative group, which is $\mathbb Z$ by the disk pair sequence and the circle homology in [F2]. Its positive disk class restricts to the positive generator at either point by [F4]. Thus every class has the same integer coefficient at those two points. Connectedness of the interior makes the integer one constant $a_D$. Subtracting $a_D$ times the relative orientation class gives zero at every interior point, hence is zero: adding the relative orientation class gives that same class back by its uniqueness in [F4]. Conversely its orientation class has local value one, so has infinite order. This also covers a closed component when $C$ is empty. [F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

It follows that if an integral one-cycle $c$ supported on the disjoint circles $C$ vanishes in $H_1(\Sigma;\mathbb Z)$, then it is the oriented boundary of an integral sum of the complementary components. Indeed the exact pair sequence [F3] lifts its class in $H_1(C;\mathbb Z)$ to $H_2(\Sigma,C;\mathbb Z)$. Step2.1 expresses that class as the finite integral sum of cut-component orientation classes. Their connectors are their oriented circle boundaries, by [F4]. Equality in $H_1(C;\mathbb Z)$ is equality of their circle coefficients, because the homology of a disjoint finite union of circles has one integral generator for each oriented circle; the circle calculation is the $S^1$ case of [F2], and finite disjointness splits the singular chain complex. Returning the collars to zero width therefore gives precisely $c=\partial\sum a_DD$ as an identity of full oriented curve coefficients. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Write $\partial P=c_\alpha+c_\beta$, separating the full-curve coefficients of the two systems. The formal region domain gives an actual relative chain on the surface: separate its finitely many cornered region closures, round corners in small vertex disks, take their relative orientation chains from [F4], and cancel paired edge boundaries; the remaining short corner arcs fill in those vertex disks. Thus $[c_\alpha]+[c_\beta]=0$ in its first homology. Also $c_\alpha$ bounds the corresponding integral combination of compression disks in $U_\alpha$, and $c_\beta$ bounds its combination in $U_\beta$. Thus $[c_\alpha]=-[c_\beta]$ belongs to both kernels in step1.1, and both classes are zero. Apply step3.1 separately to obtain integral sums $P_\alpha=\sum a_iA_i$ and $P_\beta=\sum b_iB_i$ with boundaries $c_\alpha,c_\beta$. The domain $P-P_\alpha-P_\beta$ has zero boundary. Across every attaching-curve edge its adjacent coefficients are therefore equal. A path between any two region interiors can be perturbed off the finitely many curve intersections and transverse to the finitely many embedded curve arcs it meets; in their compact smooth neighborhoods this requires only finitely many small path changes. Following it shows equality of all region coefficients, since $\Sigma$ is connected. Hence this difference is an integral multiple of the whole surface. Absorb that multiple into every $a_i$, using $\sum_iA_i=\Sigma$. This proves the asserted representation for every domain allowed by the broader Definition. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

At $w_i$ the representation has coefficient $a_i+b_i$. At $z_i$ it has coefficient $a_i+b_{i-1}$, by the cyclic indexing in [F1]. If every $w$ coefficient is zero, then $b_i=-a_i$ and $n_{z_i}=a_i-a_{i-1}$. The sum of these differences is zero. If every difference vanishes, cyclic connectedness gives one constant $a$ with every $a_i=a$ and $b_i=-a$, so $$P=a\sum_iA_i-a\sum_iB_i=a\Sigma-a\Sigma=0.$$ Otherwise a finite integer list of sum zero with at least one nonzero entry must have a positive and a negative entry. These entries occur at actual marked-region interiors, so $P$ has both a positive and a negative region coefficient. This is exactly admissibility. [F1, step 4.1, algebra, cases]

If $k=1$, the sole difference is zero and the only $w$-zero periodic domain is zero. If $m=h+k-1=0$, the attaching systems are empty, $\Sigma$ is the sphere and the same constant-domain argument applies; the relative calculation in step2.1 includes this case. Multiple marked points in one region, if they occur, introduce no exception: their coefficients are still the same integers evaluated by the displayed formulas. Finally any valid balanced knot-preserving move sequence has the same one-component cyclic marking at each stage and still splits $S^3$. Applying the result individually to its finitely many stages proves the last assertion without constructing or assuming any additional diagram moves. All sums and collar constructions are finite, and the quoted homology suppliers require no stronger choice. [F1, step 2.1, step 5.1, cases] ∎
