citations.quote: Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, put $q:=\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1$, and let
$m$ be a Mihlin symbol with constants $C_\alpha$, $|\alpha|\le q$
([[def-mihlin-symbol-with-more-than-half-dimension-derivatives]]); put
$A:=\max_{|\alpha|\le q}C_\alpha$, so that $\|m\|_\infty\le C_0\le A$. Then $m$
is an $L^p$ Fourier multiplier for every $1<p<\infty$
([[def-lp-fourier-multiplier-and-multiplier-norm]]), and there is a constant
$C_n$, depending only on $n$, with
$$\|m\|_{M_p}\le C_n\max\bigl(p,(p-1)^{-1}\bigr)\bigl(A+\|m\|_\infty\bigr) \qquad(1<p<\infty).$$
Equivalently, the operator $T_m$ of
[[def-translation-invariant-fourier-multiplier-on-schwartz-space]] satisfies
$\|T_mf\|_p\le C_n\max(p,(p-1)^{-1})(A+\|m\|_\infty)\|f\|_p$ for every
$f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. Only strict-range bounds are asserted: no
endpoint $p=1$ or $p=\infty$ claim is made.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p>2$, $\alpha=1-2/p$, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space. Every $f\in W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^2;V)$ has a unique continuous representative, and
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le C_{p,V}|x-y|^\alpha\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^2)}.$$
The same holds on the closed upper half-plane, with its gradient norm and a possibly larger constant. On a disk $B_{2r}$, or upper half-disk $B_{2r}^+$ including its straight boundary, a $W^{1,p}$ map has a continuous representative on the smaller closed disk or half-disk and satisfies
$$\|f\|_{L^\infty(B_r^{(+)})}+r^\alpha[f]_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_r^{(+)}})}\le C_{p,V}\bigl(r^{-2/p}\|f\|_{L^p(B_{2r}^{(+)})}+r^{1-2/p}\|\nabla f\|_{L^p(B_{2r}^{(+)})}\bigr).$$
The same local conclusion applied to the weak first derivatives implies that a $W^{2,p}$ map has a $C^{1,\alpha}$ representative locally, including the straight boundary.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

If $T\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\Delta T=0$, there is a unique smooth harmonic $h$ with $T=T_h$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

derivations.claim: Define $K(z)=1/(\pi z)$ as a locally integrable kernel. Its distributional derivative is $\partial_{\bar z}K=\delta_0$. Here is a direct sign and normalization check, requiring no stronger-choice Stokes theorem. For a compactly supported smooth test $\psi$, use $z=re^{i\theta}$ and $\partial_{\bar z}=e^{i\theta}(\partial_r+i r^{-1}\partial_\theta)/2$. Then $$-\int K\partial_{\bar z}\psi\,dA=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty\bigl(\psi_r+i r^{-1}\psi_\theta\bigr)\,dr\,d\theta=\psi(0).$$ The angular term integrates to zero by periodicity; it is integrable near zero because $\psi_\theta=O(r)$. For bounded $f$ supported in a disk of radius $r$, set $Tf=K*f$. On that disk, $\|Tf\|_\infty\le4r\|f\|_\infty$ by enclosing the translated integration region in the radius-$2r$ disk and integrating $1/(\pi|z|)$. This map is continuous even for measurable $f$: cut the kernel inside a small radius, whose integral norm is arbitrarily small, and use uniform continuity of the remaining nonsingular translated kernel on bounded sets. Distributional convolution gives $\partial_{\bar z}Tf=f$. [given, construct, algebra]

We prove the actual Sobolev regularity of this transform. For smooth compactly supported $f$, $H_j=\partial_jTf=K*(\partial_jf)$ is continuous, bounded on compact sets, and $O(|z|^{-2})$ at infinity. The last bound follows by subtracting $K(z)\int\partial_jf=0$ and the estimate $|K(z-\zeta)-K(z)|\le C|\zeta|/|z|^2$ outside twice the support radius. Thus $H_j\in L^2$. The distributional identity $DH_j=2\partial_jf$, Fourier differentiation and [F1] give $$\widehat H_j(\xi)=\frac{2i\xi_j}{i\xi_s-\xi_t}\widehat f(\xi)\quad\text{a.e.}$$ with Fourier convention $\widehat{\partial_j}=2\pi i\xi_j$. This follows first against Schwartz tests by integration by parts and then in $L^2$; the denominator is nonzero except at the measure-zero origin, so there is no unsupported point-mass term in this $L^2$ identity. Each displayed symbol is smooth homogeneous of degree zero with its first two derivatives bounded on the unit circle. Therefore [F1] gives $\|\nabla Tf\|_q\le C_q\|f\|_q$ for every $1<q<\infty$. For bounded compactly supported $f$, use mollified compact approximants from [F2], converging simultaneously in $L^2$ and any fixed $L^q$, $q>2$. Their transforms converge uniformly on compact sets: Hölder bounds the kernel there in $L^{q'}$, because $q'<2$. Their derivatives converge in $L^q$ by the multiplier estimate. Hence $Tf\in W^{1,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with the same weak derivative formulas. This holds for every finite $q>2$ and for matrix entries as well. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Work on a small closed disk about $z_0$ where $\|B\|_\infty$ is bounded. Define a measurable complex-linear matrix $$C(z)=-\frac{(B(z)v(z))v(z)^*}{2|v(z)|^2}$$ when $v(z)\ne0$, and zero otherwise. It satisfies $Cv=-Bv/2$ everywhere almost surely and $\|C\|\le\|B\|/2$. Thus $\partial_{\bar z}v=Cv$. Extend $C$ by zero off this disk. On continuous complex matrix functions on its closure use $\mathcal T(P)=I+T(CP)$. step 1.1 makes its contraction constant at most $4r\|C\|_\infty$. Shrink $r$ to make this less than $1/4$. Iterating from $I$ is an explicit uniformly Cauchy sequence: successive differences have geometric bounds. Its continuous limit $P$ satisfies $P=I+T(CP)$, with $\|P-I\|<1/3$, hence is pointwise invertible by its finite-matrix Neumann series. step 2.1 proves $P\in W^{1,q}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $q>2$ and $\partial_{\bar z}P=CP$. No measurable choice of matrix extensions has occurred: the formula for $C$ is specified also at the zeros. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

The inverse matrix belongs to the same local Sobolev spaces. Indeed $P^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}(I-P)^n$ converges uniformly, and its differentiated terms have $L^q$ norms bounded by $n(1/3)^{n-1}\|dP\|_q$ on compact subsets. Thus the series converges in $W^{1,q}$ and proves $d(P^{-1})=-P^{-1}(dP)P^{-1}$. The weak product rule follows by the mollifier approximation and the bounded continuous factors; the same argument or [F2] gives $h=P^{-1}v\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Since $P$ is complex linear, the ordinary matrix product rule for $\partial_{\bar z}$ gives $\partial_{\bar z}h=-P^{-1}CP\,P^{-1}v+P^{-1}Cv=0$. Thus $\Delta h=4\partial_z\partial_{\bar z}h=0$ distributionally. By [F3] it is smooth, and its now classical Cauchy–Riemann equation makes it holomorphic. Replacing $P$ by $P P(z_0)^{-1}$ and $h$ by $P(z_0)h$ gives the stated normalization without changing the factorization. [F2, F3, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

We detail finite order without a stronger-choice complex-analysis supplier. Hence $a_n(r)=c_nr^n$. Boundedness near the center forces every negative coefficient to vanish. At a fixed smaller radius $R$, $|a_n(R)|\le\sup_{|z|=R}|h|$, so $\sum_{n\ge0}c_nz^n$ converges uniformly on any still smaller disk by a geometric series. Circle Fourier completeness in [F3] identifies it with $h$ there. Apply this componentwise. Either all vector coefficients vanish, or their least nonzero index $k$ exists and $$h(z_0+z)=z^k(a+O(z)),\qquad a\ne0.$$ The continuous invertible factor from step 4.1 and its locally bounded inverse give the two-sided norm bound stated for $v$. For the variable principal structure, choose fixed real coordinates making $J(z_0)=i$ and set $\Phi(z)=(I-J(z)i)/2$. Finally take two smooth solutions $u_1,u_2$ with equal value at an interior point and use a convex target coordinate ball near that value. The variable-principal result therefore applies. Equal infinite jets give infinite-order zero of $w$ and force equality locally. If the two maps agree on an open set, the same local argument propagates equality to its closure, and connectedness gives global equality. In the infinite-jet case first obtain that nonempty equality neighborhood and propagate it. This completes the similarity and unique-continuation assertions. [step 5.1, step 6.1, construct, algebra] ∎

Assume countable choice and write $D=\partial_s+i\partial_t=2\partial_{\bar z}$ on a connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb C$. Let $B\in L^\infty_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb R}(\mathbb C^m))$, and let $v\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb C^m)$, for some $p>2$, solve $Dv+Bv=0$ weakly. Use its continuous representative. Near every point $z_0$ there are a continuous invertible complex matrix $P$, belonging locally to $W^{1,q}$ for every finite $q>2$, and a holomorphic vector function $h$ with $v=Ph$. One may normalize $P(z_0)=I$.

Consequently either $v$ is identically zero, or all its zeros are isolated and have finite order: at a zero $z_0$ there are an integer $k\ge1$ and constants $c,C,r>0$ with
$$c|z-z_0|^k\le|v(z)|\le C|z-z_0|^k\qquad(0<|z-z_0|<r).$$
In particular vanishing on an open set, or vanishing to infinite order at one point, forces global vanishing. The same conclusions hold for $v_s+J(s,t)v_t+Av=0$ when $J$ is a smooth family of real complex structures and $A$ is locally bounded; the local factor is then an invertible real matrix rather than necessarily a complex matrix.

If two smooth maps solve the same equation $u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0$ for a smooth almost complex family on a smooth target and have matching infinite jets at one interior point, they agree everywhere on their connected common source. Agreement on an open set suffices. This assertion concerns parametrized maps and actual linear equations; it does not infer moduli transversality or an injective-point theorem.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,g)$ be compact, let $L_0,L_1\subset X$ be compact smooth half-dimensional submanifolds with finite intersection, and let $J(s,t,x)$ be smooth almost complex structures on $[0,\infty)\times[0,1]\times X$ with uniform $C^2$ bounds in source and target. Assume $J(s,j,x)=J_{b,j}(x)$ for $x\in L_j$, independent of $s$, and that $L_j$ is totally real for $J_{b,j}$. A smooth solution
$$u_s+J(s,t,u)u_t=0,\qquad u(s,j)\in L_j,$$
with finite Dirichlet energy has a unique point $x_+\in L_0\cap L_1$ such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le1}d_g(u(s,t),x_+)\longrightarrow0,\qquad \sup_{0\le t\le1}|du(s,t)|_g\longrightarrow0$$
as $s\to\infty$. In particular no such strip exists if $L_0\cap L_1$ is empty. Compact transverse half-dimensional $L_0,L_1$ satisfy the finite-intersection premise. The analogous conclusion holds at a negative strip end. No exponential rate or index theorem is asserted.

derivations.claim: Differentiate the actual equation in $s$. The section $\eta=u_s$ satisfies $$\eta_s+J_t(u)\eta_t+(d_xJ_t)_u[\eta]u_t=0.$$ In target charts this is precisely the smooth variable-principal linear equation of [F1]. It cannot vanish identically: if $u_s=0$, the equation forces $u_t=0$ and the map is constant. Thus its zero set $Z$ is discrete in the interior. For any fixed $a\in K$, comparison with the constant solution $u\equiv a$ in [F1] likewise shows $u^{-1}(a)$ is discrete, since $u$ is nonconstant. Consequently $Z\cup u^{-1}(K)$ is locally finite and has empty interior. Its complement is open: these are zeros of continuous sections and a finite union of closed point-preimages. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

We supply the elementary Baire fact needed below without importing a theorem assuming dependent choice. A nonempty Euclidean open rectangle cannot be a countable union of relatively closed sets with empty interior. Otherwise start with a closed rational ball compactly inside it. Enumerate rational balls once and, at stage $n$, take the first one whose closure lies in the preceding ball's interior minus the $n$th closed set, with radius less than $2^{-n}$. Such a ball exists because the excluded set has empty interior and rational balls form a base. This rule is deterministic, so recursion needs no dependent choice. The nested centers are Cauchy; completeness gives a point lying in every closed ball and outside every listed set, a contradiction. A discrete subset of the interior strip is countable as well: assign each point the first rational basis rectangle containing it but no other point of the set. Different points receive different rectangles, so this is an injection into a countable set. [given, construct, algebra]

Put $F(s,t)=(t,u(s,t))\in(0,1)\times X$. Off $Z$ this is an immersion and locally an embedding. Indeed some coordinate component $u_j$ has $(u_j)_s\ne0$, and the derivative of $(s,t)\mapsto(t,u_j(s,t))$ is invertible. Apply [F2]; the remaining target coordinates are then graphs over these two. Fix a small open rectangle $U$ with compact closure in the regular complement from step 1.1, on which $F$ is an embedding, and a smaller nonempty open rectangle $U_0$ compactly inside $U$. The values $u(\overline U_0)$ have positive distance from $K$, and its time coordinates stay in a compact subinterval of $(0,1)$. Uniform end convergence therefore gives $S<\infty$ such that every partner $q$ with $F(q)=F(p)$, $p\in U_0$, lies in the fixed compact strip rectangle $[-S,S]\times[\epsilon,1-\epsilon]$. A distinct partner cannot lie in $U$, by its embedding property. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Suppose $\mathcal R(u)$ were not dense. Choose $U,U_0$ as in step 2.1 inside an open set without points of $\mathcal R(u)$. Every $p\in U_0$ has a distinct partner. Critical partners belong to the countable set $Z$ by the discrete-zero observation and countability argument above; their contributions are contained in the countably many horizontal lines $t=t(q)$, which are relatively closed sets with empty interior in $U_0$. For regular partners use all closed rational rectangles $C_j$ disjoint from $U_0$ and compactly contained in a regular coordinate-embedding neighborhood of step 2.1. They form a countable collection covering every regular point outside $U$: each has a smaller rational rectangle inside its embedding neighborhood and outside $\overline U_0$. The sets $$E_j=\{p\in U_0:F(p)\in F(C_j)\}$$ are relatively closed, since $F(C_j)$ is compact in the Hausdorff target. Together with the critical-partner horizontal lines they cover $U_0$. Step 1.2 implies one $E_j$ has nonempty interior $W$. Shrink $W$ to a connected open rectangle. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

On $W$ there is a unique smooth partner $q=H(p)$ in that $C_j$. The inverse on $F(C_j)$ is continuous because $C_j$ is compact and the target is Hausdorff. Smoothness then follows locally from the local inverse to the two coordinate components in step 2.1 on its embedding neighborhood; composition with those components of $F(p)$ gives the inverse also at boundary points of $C_j$. Since its first target component is $t$, write $H(s,t)=(\sigma(s,t),t)$. Equality of the maps gives $$u_s(p)=u_s(q)\sigma_s,\qquad u_t(p)=u_s(q)\sigma_t+u_t(q).$$ Both points solve the same equation with the same $t$ and target value. Subtracting yields $$u_s(q)(\sigma_s-1)+J_t(u(q))u_s(q)\sigma_t=0.$$ The two displayed real vectors are independent: a nonzero vector and its image under a real complex structure cannot be real dependent. Thus $\sigma_s=1$ and $\sigma_t=0$, so $\sigma=s+c$ for one constant $c\ne0$. The constant is nonzero because $C_j\cap U_0=\varnothing$. Hence $u(s+c,t)=u(s,t)$ on $W$. By [F1], the shifted map is the same solution on the entire connected interior strip; continuity extends this to the physical edges. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

This nonzero longitudinal period is impossible. The energy density is periodic with period $|c|$. Its integral on a single period times the whole physical interval is either positive, giving infinite total energy by summing disjoint periods, or zero. In the latter case the smooth nonnegative density is zero everywhere, forcing the map constant. Both alternatives contradict the hypotheses. Thus the assumed open set without $\mathcal R(u)$ cannot exist, and density is proved. [step 4.1, given, algebra]

Finally $\mathcal R(u)$ is open. If $p_n\to p\in\mathcal R(u)$ but $p_n$ has a distinct same-time partner $q_n$, uniform ends and $u(p)\notin K$ bound their longitudinal coordinates as in step 2.1. Their time coordinates stay interior, so a subsequence converges to a point $q$ with $F(q)=F(p)$. Injectivity at $p$ gives $q=p$. For large $n$ both $p_n,q_n$ then lie in one embedding neighborhood of $F$ at $p$, a contradiction. The other two defining conditions persist by continuity. This proves openness. The actual boundary-setting application follows from [F3] and the just proved argument; no boundary regularity or universal surjectivity was silently added. Work in the smooth category inherited from the oriented-link convention. In particular, an embedded bridge witness disk means the image of a smooth rank-two embedding of a planar disk, with ordinary smooth boundary or smooth transverse corners at its two marked endpoints; smoothness at a boundary or corner means local smooth extension in its charts. Witness parametrizations can be chosen for the finite disk families. This category convention does not require the knot arcs to meet the Heegaard surface transversely: tangential smooth crossings remain permitted.

Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $h$, let $k\ge1$, and put $m=h+k-1$. A **handlebody** is a compact three-manifold that is a regular neighborhood of a finite connected graph. A **$2k$-pointed Heegaard diagram for $S^3$** consists of a splitting $S^3=U_{\alpha}\cup_{\Sigma}U_{\beta}$ into handlebodies, two systems $\boldsymbol\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m)$ and $\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$ of pairwise disjoint simple closed curves on $\Sigma$ that bound pairwise disjoint properly embedded disks in $U_{\alpha}$ and $U_{\beta}$, respectively, cutting each handlebody into exactly $k$ three-balls, and two ordered sets of distinct points $\mathbf w=(w_1,\ldots,w_k)$ and $\mathbf z=(z_1,\ldots,z_k)$ disjoint from the curves. Curves from different systems intersect transversely in finitely many points. Each component of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$ contains exactly one $w$-point and exactly one $z$-point. The diagram also includes trivial arc systems in the two handlebodies: the $\alpha$-arcs join $w_i$ to $z_i$, and the $\beta$-arcs join $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$, with indices modulo $k$. Each system is disjoint from its compression disks and is simultaneously boundary parallel: its arcs cobound pairwise disjoint embedded disks with arcs in the corresponding components of the attaching-system complement on $\Sigma$. Thus each ball obtained by compression contains one unknotted arc. Together the arcs form an oriented knot, oriented from $w_i$ to $z_i$ in $U_{\alpha}$ and from $z_i$ to $w_{i-1}$ in $U_{\beta}$. The diagram is **compatible with $K$** when this knot is orientation-preservingly ambient isotopic to $K$. For a grid diagram, compatibility uses the row and column orientation fixed in the grid definition, with $w$-points at $O$ and $z$-points at $X$. For a grid representing one knot, the basepoint pairs can be numbered cyclically in reverse order of travel along the oriented knot so that $w_i,z_i$ lie in the same component $A_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\alpha$ and $w_i,z_{i+1}$ lie in the same component $B_i$ of $\Sigma\setminus\boldsymbol\beta$.

Comparisons of these embedded diagrams allow **orientation-preserving diagram isomorphisms**: an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of $S^3$ carrying the two handlebodies, their oriented Heegaard surface, the two attaching systems, the ordered $w,z$ points, and the two simultaneously boundary-parallel arc systems to the corresponding data. Equivalently one may specify the surface isomorphism together with its compatible collared extensions over both handlebodies carrying those arcs. The attaching systems are carried as systems; reordering their curve factors induces the corresponding product identification. Comparisons also allow **arc normalizations in the fixed splitting**: a smooth isotopy of the represented oriented knot, supported near the ordered marks and fixing each mark, during which every open connecting arc stays in its original handlebody and the two simultaneous boundary-parallel witness systems are retained or replaced by embedded witnesses for those same arcs. The surface, attaching curves, marked points and compression disks stay fixed. Such a normalization may replace a tangential marked crossing by a transverse one; the original data are not required to have neat arcs. This is a change of knot representative relative to the fixed surface, not a diagram isomorphism carrying both objects. Analytic and assigned grading data depending on the fixed surface diagram can be kept identical; the corresponding generator and disk-count identification is then the identity. Existence of normalizations with the required witnesses is a separate geometric assertion, not part of this definition. Such a comparison transports the represented oriented knot and any specified Seifert surface as well. For analytic data, it transports $j$, the surface area form, all chosen divisor neighborhoods and $J_t$ by the induced symmetric-product diffeomorphism. The comparison maps on generators and disk classes are their pushforwards under this map; compatibility with the count differential is a mathematical property to be proved. No identity action is part of this convention, even when the ambient diffeomorphism is isotopic to the identity.

The $m$-fold symmetric product $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)=\Sigma^m/S_m$ is the space of unordered $m$-tuples of points of $\Sigma$, where $S_m$ permutes coordinates. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ be the quotient map. The product tori are the images $\mathbb T_{\alpha}=q(\alpha_1\times\cdots\times\alpha_m)$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}=q(\beta_1\times\cdots\times\beta_m)$. Their intersection points are the generators. A **Whitney disk class** $\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a relative homotopy class of maps from a disk to $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ whose two boundary arcs lie on $\mathbb T_{\alpha}$ and $\mathbb T_{\beta}$ and whose endpoints are $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf y$. Its domain is the integral two-chain of complementary regions with coefficients equal to local multiplicities. Write $n_{w_i}(\phi)$ and $n_{z_i}(\phi)$ for its local multiplicities at the marked points. An almost complex structure $J$ on $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ is a smooth endomorphism of the tangent bundle with $J^2=-1$. Fix a complex structure $j$ and an area form on $\Sigma$. For $m>0$, choose a smooth path $\mathbb J=(J_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ of nearly symmetric almost complex structures, constant near $t=0,1$: each $J_t$ agrees with the induced integrable structure $\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(j)$ on a fixed neighborhood of the diagonal and of every divisor $\{p\}+\operatorname{Sym}^{m-1}(\Sigma)$ for a chosen interior point $p$ of every complementary region, including every marked point, and tames the form descended from the product area form off that neighborhood. The path is a sufficiently small perturbation in this class. For $m=0$ the symmetric product is a point. Local multiplicities are intersection numbers with these divisors; positivity is a mathematical property to be proved, not an additional choice of disk counts. A $\mathbb J$-holomorphic strip representative is a smooth map $u:\mathbb R\times[0,1]\to\operatorname{Sym}^{m}(\Sigma)$ satisfying $\partial_{\tau}u+J_t(u)\partial_tu=0$, with $u(\tau,0)\in\mathbb T_{\alpha}$, $u(\tau,1)\in\mathbb T_{\beta}$, and limits $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$ as $\tau\to-\infty,+\infty$. Translation in $\tau$ defines an $\mathbb R$-action. The Maslov index $\mu(\phi)$ is the Fredholm index of the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at a representative of $\phi$; the relative Maslov grading convention is $M(\mathbf x)-M(\mathbf y)=\mu(\phi)-2\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_{w_i}(\phi)$, up to one overall additive constant.

A **periodic domain** is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of full $\alpha$- and $\beta$-curves; its local multiplicity at a marked point is the coefficient of the containing region. The pointed diagram is **admissible** when every nonzero periodic domain with $n_{w_i}=0$ for all $i$ has at least one positive and at least one negative region coefficient. A path $\mathbb J$ is **regular for a set of disk classes** when the linearized Cauchy–Riemann operator at every holomorphic-strip representative in those classes is surjective. For a path regular on the classes used, let $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)$ be the space of strip representatives. If, for each generator $\mathbf x$, only finitely many pairs $(\mathbf y,\phi)$ with $\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing$, $\mu(\phi)=1$, and $n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0$ for every $i$ occur, and each quotient is finite, the multipointed full filtered minus module is the free module over $\mathbb F_2[U_1,\ldots,U_k]$ generated by $\mathbb T_{\alpha}\cap\mathbb T_{\beta}$, with differential
$$\partial^-\mathbf x=\sum_{\mathbf y}\sum_{\substack{\phi\in\pi_2(\mathbf x,\mathbf y),\;\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)\ne\varnothing\\\mu(\phi)=1,\; n_{w_i}(\phi)\ge0\ \forall i}}\#_2\bigl(\mathcal M_{\mathbb J}(\phi)/\mathbb R\bigr)\,U_1^{n_{w_1}(\phi)}\cdots U_k^{n_{w_k}(\phi)}\mathbf y.$$
Here $\#_2$ is the count modulo two of the zero-dimensional quotient when it is finite. Quotienting by all $U_i$ leaves the fully blocked multipointed chain complex (the hat chain complex when $k=1$), with terms only from classes satisfying $n_{w_i}=0$ for every $i$; its Alexander-filtered associated-graded complex further retains only classes with every $n_{z_i}=0$. The relative Alexander grading convention is $A(\mathbf x)-A(\mathbf y)=\sum_i n_{z_i}(\phi)-\sum_i n_{w_i}(\phi)$, with an overall additive constant. Each $U_i$ lowers Maslov grading by two and Alexander filtration by one. In a grid diagram, $\Sigma=T^2$, $h=1$, $k=n$, and $m=n$; the horizontal circles are the $\alpha$-curves, the vertical circles are the $\beta$-curves, and the $w$-points and $z$-points are the $O$- and $X$-markings respectively.
